speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the failure of the Minister of National Defence to disclose to the house during consideration of his estimates a hidden report of the Department of Finance asserting that many thousands of men were already being wasted in the navy, army and air force.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLEGED WASTE OF MANPOWER
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I have been asked by the hon. member for Laurier for leave under standing order 26 to move the adjournment of the house for the discussion of a subject which is certainly not the usual type of subject advanced as requiring the postponement of other proceedings and as being of such general public importance to permit a discussion under the standing order.
What the hon. member wishes to discuss is the alleged failure of the Minister of National Defence to disclose what is referred to as a hidden report in the course of the consideration of his estimates. In other words the complaint is about some action that did not take place, or some act within the House of Commons itself. These matters are usually dealt with as questions of privilege if they involve the privileges of the house, or as a matter of grievance if it is a complaint against the conduct of the government in its actions toward the house.
I think it would be improper to extend the scope of the rule to cover matters which are purely questions of the relationship of the minister to the house within the house.

As the house knows, the minister's estimates are now complete and have passed the house. There is no opportunity, therefore, to discuss those estimates again during the remaining time the house will be sitting. Then there is the question of the motion to go into supply. We, of our own volition, decided to forgo that motion, so there is no other occasion upon which we would have an opportunity to discuss a matter of this nature. We did this by agreement among the parties; I will not say it was done at the request of the government, but it was decided we would forgo the motion to go into supply under certain circumstances. Then there was this sensational story in the Globe and Mail of national importance. Surely there is no other opportunity from now until the end of the session when we may be given a chance to discuss a matter of this importance.
I shall not, as I say, go into the merits of the subject, Mr. Speaker, but here is a story which, if there is any foundation for it, at least calls for some explanation by the Minister of National Defence, the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance if he were here.
I should like an opportunity to discuss the merits of the subject after Your Honour has dealt with what I am now saying. As the matter stands now there will be no opportunity from now until the end of the session to discuss this matter of urgent public importance.

At any rate, even if I accepted the hon. member's argument it seems to me that the foundation of the motion is scarcely sufficient. It seems to me that he ought to establish that there is a report and that it is a report which in the public interest should be presented to parliament. That is a matter that can be brought out by questions, and the hon. member will have that opportunity. speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: STATEMENT ON ACTIVITIES OF CURRENT GENERAL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for his kind words, and I am sure the house is also very glad to welcome him back from the Middle East.
In his work with the United Nations the hon. member represented Canada in connection with the very difficult question of refugees in the Middle East. He has now had an opportunity to visit the camps and see just what is going on there, and I am sure this will be beneficial to the house.

The outstanding event of the sixteenth session of the general assembly thus far has been the tremendous impact made by the tragic death of the secretary general, Mr. Dag Hammarskjold. It would be difficult for one to express adequately just how the delegates from all countries, except perhaps the communist countries, have been saddened by this event. Tributes were paid to the memory of this great world statesman a day or two ago, and I had the privilege of speaking for Canada and also for Australia and New Zealand. We were very pleased that they asked us to say a few words on their behalf as well as on our own.
This death, of course, could be disastrous for the United Nations, coming as it did at about the worst time such an event could possibly occur. However, I believe there will be a great rallying to the support of that world organization. I believe most of the delegations are determined that the United Nations shall not be allowed to fail, and that it will go on to achieve greater strength as a result of the inspiration of Dag Hammarskjold and the sacrifice he has made in the cause of world peace.
There was no difficulty in electing a president, Mongi Slim, who has given distinguished service for Tunisia in the United Nations. Since that country achieved its independence about five years ago he has been the permanent representative of Tunisia at the United Nations. He is admired and respected by all countries. I believe he is the first African president of the United Nations. The fact that under present conditions he was elected unanimously augurs well for the future.
The immediate question, of course, is what to do about putting someone in charge of the direction of the secretariat. I believe it may take some little time to work out the election of a secretary general on the basis secretary generals have been elected in the past, but at the moment what is needed is someone to act in a temporary capacity as director of the secretariat. There is no thought of making such a man an acting secretary general and giving him that status, but he would be in charge of the work of the secretariat.
Strenuous efforts are being made to arrive at a decision which will bring about that result. Thus far the communist countries say they are going to stand firm on the troika principle, which is that there must be a three-headed supervision with one representative of the western countries, one of the communist countries and one of the uncommitted countries. I think there is no support whatever for that suggestion, either on an acting basis or on a permanent basis, outside the nine communist countries, and two of
Inquiries of the Ministry those communist countries are Byelorussia and the Ukraine. Possibly Cuba might support it, but I believe every Afro-Asian country is against the troika principle. We had a meeting of the commonwealth representatives on Wednesday morning and every one of the commonwealth delegations is against any such principle.
I am hoping that within a very few days some arrangement can be worked out so that a temporary director can be appointed. This would be done in the general assembly, not subject to recommendation from the security council, as would be the case if a secretary general were to be appointed which, of course, would give the Soviet union an opportunity to veto anything proposed in the security council.
I believe there has been quite a reduction in tension during the last two or three weeks. I have always been of the opinion that a meeting of the United Nations assembly would bring about a reduction of tension, and I think it is doing that. It is very significant that the United States and the Soviet union agreed just a day or two ago-I get all mixed up about days; things move rather rapidly in the United Nations-on a statement of principles for disarmament. These are the principles that will form the background of an actual negotiated agreement on the details of disarmament.
I expect that on Monday President Kennedy will announce a revised disarmament plan, in the preparation of which Canada has had a very important part. Many of our suggestions have been written into this proposal, and I think hon. members will find it is the most appealing disarmament proposal which has yet been advanced. There still remains the question of the forum in which the negotiations would take place, whether it would be in the old 10 nation committee of which Canada is a member, or be in the 10 nation committee plus three officers from unaligned countries which we suggested last year, or whether it would be in the 10 nation committee plus 10 uncommitted countries which the United States has also suggested, or whether it would be referred to the disarmament commission of the United Nations. This question of forum will have to be worked out, and I hope Canada will be able to take some initiative in connection with that particular problem.
On the question of Berlin, Secretary of State Rusk and Mr. Gromyko, the foreign minister of the Soviet union met a day or two ago and they are to meet again next week. They are discussing possible negotiations on the Berlin question. It does not do for one to be too optimistic on any of these questions; I learned this the hard way. Some

Inquiries of the Ministry people in Canada believe the foreign minister should not be too optimistic. However, I believe there is a reasonable chance that negotiations on the question of Berlin can be arranged, and we hope to have something to say on this Berlin question ourselves when Canada participates in the general debate which is now taking place.
I have had the privilege of holding discussions with several other foreign ministers. The hon. member for Essex East knows that the United Nations is about the best place possible for foreign ministers to exchange views. I plan to go back on Thursday night, or perhaps Wednesday night, and continue with such conferences, and I believe our statement will be made perhaps a week from Tuesday. In any event, I suggest to the house that there is no need to give up hope for the United Nations. I think it is going to come out of this crisis stronger than it has ever been. I remain convinced that it is the one hope of mankind.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief observations on a matter which I probably could not bring up on any other item in the Prime Minister's estimates. I am not going to say anything about the administration of the office. What I am going to do is make an appeal to the Prime Minister with respect to a matter about which I think he told the house he has reached an understanding with the premier of Newfoundland

certainly there was a public announcement-with respect to the title of the former United States air force base at Fort Pepperrell on the outskirts of the city of St. John's, Newfoundland. I want to emphasize that in what I have to say I am speaking for myself solely, as a member of parliament, and that I am in no way making any plea for any other person whatever. I am seeking to do this in a noncontentious spirit. I do not intend to make any attempt whatever to argue the legal case, because I feel it would be a quite improper use of the time of the committee to do anything of that sort.
The case I want to make very briefly to the Prime Minister is this; that notwithstanding any question as to whether there may or may not be a claim to federal title, there is no compelling reason why the federal authority should seek to get possession of

Supply-Privy Council this property. This was not military property of the British government or the Newfoundland government; it was a property that was acquired out of crown lands or private lands in Newfoundland by the then commission of government of Newfoundland to be turned over as a free gift by the British government to the United States on a 99 year lease, in the darkest days of the war. This territory, according to the agreement that was made at that time, was to revert to Newfoundland at the end of the 99 years or at any earlier time at which the lease might be terminated.
It is true, of course, that the ultimate title to anything which was vested in Newfoundland before union, has to be construed in relation to the terms of union; because when Newfoundland became a part of Canada that legal entity of Newfoundland was divided between the government of the province and the government of Canada. I am not seeking to found any legal argument there. What I am suggesting is, here is a very valuable piece of real estate which was, in no way, a military base. It never was a military base even in the sense in which Harmon field and Argentia were military establishments. Fort Pepperrell was not anything but a headquarters. Most of the buildings there are buildings that could and would be put to a civilian use.
For over a year now this valuable property has been unoccupied. It is costing both the provincial and federal treasuries a certain amount annually to keep it up. There are many parts of this establishment for which the provincial government, either directly or through the local authorities, could undoubtedly find a use. Moreover, whatever may be the legal niceties of the matter, there would seem to be an incontrovertible moral claim on the part of the people and province of Newfoundland to the restitution to them of this territory which was taken for exceptional emergency purposes, not Canadian purposes or British purposes or Newfoundland purposes but United States purposes. This was done at a time when everybody was quite prepared to justify it.
The suggestion I am making to the Prime Minister is one about which I am quite sure there would be no criticism in any part of this country. I am not criticizing the decision to refer the matter to the supreme court because, in itself, I think that is a very appropriate way of dealing with a problem of this sort. However, if the federal government were to decide that in view of the unique situation here no precedent that could be embarrassing in other situations would arise or could arise, it could unilaterally declare it was no longer interested in asserting any title to this property, then some means could

be found, perhaps by a special act of parliament, of validating the title of the province to this territory. It was made clear during the discussion of the defence estimates that there was no military necessity for acquiring this property.
I believe, and I hope, that such action would be regarded by everyone as a proper disposition of this matter. Even if an announcement were made that such action was going to be taken, and custody were transferred on that basis, this would enable this valuable property to be used effectively immediately. As I say, I am putting this suggestion forward in, I hope, a completely noncontentious spirit. I have no criticism at all of anything the government has done. I am merely suggesting a course of action which I feel would commend itself to most Canadians.
I might venture, perhaps, an analogy. The privy council established that Indian reserves, so long as they are used for the purpose for which they were taken in the first place, they are under the ultimate control of the government of Canada through the superintendent general. However, if an Indian band becomes extinct, the title to that land immediately reverts to the province and does not remain in the crown in the right of Canada.
It seems to me if that is true of Indian lands, some of which may have been Indian reserves for more than a hundred years, then the same principle could be applied to this land. In British Columbia recently there was a case of an Indian reserve which had been established in 1871, or whenever Indian reserves were established shortly after the union of British Columbia with Canada, and the band became extinct. The title to the land was immediately transferred to the province without any question, and it became provincial crown land. There have been a good many other cases of this kind.
I recognize at once that the Prime Minister could not, and properly would not, himself give a snap judgment on a suggestion of this sort. All I am doing is putting forward this suggestion and asking if he will give it most sympathetic consideration. He could discuss with his colleagues whether or not this course would be in the national interest and in the interest of maintaining that harmony we all wish to see prevail, particularly in the light of the fact there is certainly no clear and specific language in the terms of union dealing with this matter, presumably because those who drafted the terms did not feel any provision of that kind was necessary. There may have been the feeling that the normal presumptions would apply in this matter. I say, having put this suggestion to the Prime Minister, all I am asking him to>
do today is

to say that it will be given sympathetic consideration, and I hope he will do this.

As I listened to the hon. gentleman, I could not but regret that he had decided to discontinue his studies leading to admission to the bar. He made his argument in a very objective manner. He, of course, frankly admitted that he was speaking for himself alone, and that no one else apparently held the same view or at least had impressed him as to holding that view.
As I recollect it, the premier of Newfoundland at one of the dominion-provincial conferences asked that this matter be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada. That was at his request. I seem to recall he said that the legal argument that the lands should be vested in the people of Newfoundland was unchallengeable. Arrangements were then made that the question of the rights of the two governments in respect to this property be referred to the supreme court, and the matter is now before that court. Although it has not been argued yet it is in the custody of the court. When the answers are given by that court, both governments will be in a position to know their legal rights. I think that is as far as I should wish to go at this time.

In view of the reply the Prime Minister has made, may I say that I either did not make myself clear-and that is quite possible-or the Prime Minister in a very polite way is saying that he will not consider my suggestion. I understand perfectly that the government of Canada must consider that it has some vestige of a claim or it would not have taken the responsibility of making any reference at all to the courts. The argument I was making was that whether or not there was any legal claim, in my view there did not seem to be any good moral claim or any really pressing military reason why the government should seek to assert any title in this matter.
The Prime Minister of course-he having practised law as I have not and never expect to-will know that a great many cases, even though they have been taken to the courts, have been settled out of court. What I was suggesting was this. In view of the importance of getting this property into use promptly, and in view of the fact that in common sense there is no real, national interest involved here at all, my suggestion was that the reference should be abandoned and that the government, through parliament or otherwise, could take whatever steps might be necessary in order to make sure that the title would be a valid one on the part of the crown in the right of the province.

The other day the Prime Minister in another debate-I know I cannot quote from that debate, but I am sure he will not object to my alluding to it-was good enough to make reference to an interest which I had expressed to him in the possibility of the government of Canada acquiring Earnscliffe and using it as the residence of the Prime Minister instead of the present residence. I should like to say this. Although there might be some members of my party who would think that the residence of the first prime minister of Canada, because of his party, would not be a suitable residence for prime ministers of other parties, that is not a view that I would share; nor would anyone in the House of Commons, knowing how non-partisan and moderate I am in my views, expect me to share it.
Oh, oh.

I think any Liberal prime minister or any Liberal who was not willing, and would not consider it an honour, to live in the house in which Sir John Macdonald lived would not really deserve to be prime minister of Canada. There are no sentimental associations that I know of attached to the present residence of the Prime Minister. It is a beautiful place. It is perhaps in an even more pleasant physical location than Earnscliffe. I cannot think that the United Kingdom would be any loser in the bargain. I believe it would be pleasing to all Canadians if that exchange were possible. I would even go so far as to say this. I see in the chamber a member of the New Democratic party, which I am inclined to refer by with different initials. I would call them the S.O.P., or the same old party.
Oh, oh.

I note that they are largely represented in the house at the present time.
I would hope that one of their many spokesmen in the house at the present time would join me in an assurance that in the unlikely

When the clock interrupted my remarks some days ago, Mr. Chairman, I was expressing the opinion that the government's measures, although we are in agreement with the extent by which they have been increased and their velocity has been increased, still are not geared to the kind of threat with which we are faced. We are not faced with a limited nuclear war but with a massive attack of proportions completely beyond anything which, in our imagination, we could expect from our knowledge of former wars.

During the defence debates the Minister of National Defence refused to give us details of this threat, and he did so quite properly within the bounds of his privilege. However,
I cannot help but remind the government that, as was stated by the Leader of the Opposition and by the hon. member for Trinity, and as others in this House of Commons have suggested, statistics are available from United States and British sources which indicate a far different picture of that which we are either defending against or are expecting to survive. In the discussions on the defence estimates we mentioned the navy, as a part of its work and in conjunction with our allies, attempting to deal with a few conventional submarines when, of course, there may be many. Some of these will be nuclear powered, and completely beyond the capabilities of our vessels. In regard to aerial attack, we will not be dealing with a few bombers but a great many bombers. These will certainly have air to ground missiles capable of dealing with the defences that we have.
What we in this corner are attempting to get some idea about is the massive threat which exists. We feel the emergency measures organization, in the same way as the defence department, is carrying on a business as usual philosophy in connection with this whole matter of survival. In his television broadcast the other night the Prime Minister indicated to the Canadian people that he would be most frank with them in these matters of defence, foreign affairs and, I am sure, survival techniques also. I am sure the Prime Minister would not want the Canadian people to be deceived in this matter; that would be criminal. It is not in any way a scaring of the Canadian people to indicate the extent of this threat. If the defence of democracy becomes dependent upon ignorance of this threat, the defence itself will have lost all meaning because democracy will have completely gone.
Turning to the shelter program proposed by the government, I have suggested that it is based on ability to pay, which is the negation of our whole democratic system; because surely our belief is that every individual is of equal worth in the eyes of his government. I went on to read the letter of a nuclear physicist who is very concerned about this matter because of his experience as a physicist. I should like to read a few more paragraphs from this letter in which he visualizes this kind of nuclear attack.
Who is the physicist in question?

He is Mr. A. Charles Whittier, who has worked for 10 years with Atomic Energy of Canada, with the nuclear division of Canadian General Electric, and civilian atomic power development. He now has on hand two instruments, which have been patented, for the detection of radioactivity.
Mr. Pallet!: Mr. Chairman, would the hon. gentleman indicate the name of the writer?
He just did.

It is Mr. A. C. Whittier. He says in his letter:
Suppose a nuclear bomb drops a few miles away, and radioactive fall-out settles on the roof of a house. (This process generally takes between 1 and 48 hours after the explosion.) Consider first a case where the fall-out is sufficient to give a dose during a 2-week period of 10 roentgens in an unsheltered basement. In this case the occupants do not need a shelter for 10 roentgens is less than the 25 roentgens "threshold" dose. Now consider a case where the fall-out is much greater, so that the unsheltered dose would be 4,000 roentgens in 2 weeks. In this case, if the occupants had a shelter and stayed in it for 2 weeks they would receive a 400 roentgens dose:	half of
them would die in a short time, and the other half would wish they were dead. This means, then, that a shelter is only useful for protection against gamma radiation provided the dosage received in an unsheltered area is between 10 roentgens and
something considerably less than 4,000 roentgens_
say 1,000 roentgens-in 2 weeks . ..
Something like a 10 roentgens dose will arise from the fall-out from a 2.4 kiloton atom bomb if this fall-out is distributed uniformly over 1,000 square miles; 1,000 roentgens will arise from a 240 kiloton fall-out over the same area. Therefore a fall-out shelter will be useful only if the fallout density is between 2.4 and 240 kilotons per
1.000	square miles.
It has been estimated that the U.S.S.R. has the potential to mount a surprise attack that would give a uniform density of about 5,000 kilotons per
1.000	square miles over the whole of the U.S.A. Of course in an actual attack the density in some areas would be much higher, and in others much lower than 5,000. If a 1 megaton bomb were dropped, what chance is there that the fall-out density would be conveniently between 2.4 and 240 kilotons per 1,000 square miles at the house in question?
The $500 fall-out shelter has no means of filtering the air which the occupants must breathe. This air will be loaded with radioactive strontium, iodine, and other fission products. Just how lethal these would be depends on the situation.
Because of the foregoing I do not think an individual will be affecting significantly the probable lifespan of his family by spending $500 on a basement shelter.
I feel that $500 per family could be much more effectively spent if done collectively. By far the most effective protection against fall-out is afforded by large public shelters stocked with food and water, and with proper air filtering facilities. These shelters would also have medical equipment, radiation detection instruments, water purification equipment and decontamination gear, along with people qualified to use these articles.
Then he goes on to refer to a study which was made in the United States in the case of

The figures apply to those who are still alive after the blast, fireball, and immediate irradiation have passed on.
In an unprotected community, 90 per cent of the living would die. In a community full of $500 basement shelters, 80 per cent would die. In a community with shelters prepared from modified buildings-
-as the government is going on with today-
-50 per cent would die, and in a community with special fall-out shelters, less than 1 per cent would die.
This is a matter which the Canadian people should be very sure of, and I think there are a number of problems to deal with in regard to these basement shelters. The attack must take place, we assume, between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m., when people are conveniently at home. I can imagine the holocaust that would take place in a city such as Montreal or Toronto if the attack took place during the working day when people were concentrated in the centre of the city.
That is why we feel we must either prepare for the kind of war which is to come or -we are not suggesting this as an alternative -not prepare at all. It is not a matter of terrorizing but of facing the issue courageously. In other words, let us just not spend a few million dollars to create the impression that we are doing something-
Mr. Pallet!: Mr. Chairman, in the letter from which the hon. member read there was reference to a study which had been made in the United States. Did the writer identify where that study had been carried out?
No, he does not identify the area. In terms of populations, similar figures were given to United States congressional hearings.

speechtext: What was the date of the hearing?

I am sorry; I do not have that information. I will be very happy to try and obtain it.
In an article in the Ottawa Citizen of September 13 a very well-known nuclear physicist, the famous physicist of the Lawrence radiation laboratory of the University of California, Dr. Teller, gave the method by which there could be some defence against nuclear war. He was referring to national survival. Of course, he made these specific suggestions to the government of the United States, but these are the things he suggests and these are the only ways he suggests by which we can really survive a full-scale thermonuclear war. First, building shelters against fall-out and against the blast and fire

Supply-Privy Council
from nuclear bombs; second, stockpiling surplus food, machinery, machine tools, generators, building materials-the essentials to generate power, start factories, build more machines, transport people and goods, and assure communications; third, planning organized efforts to carry people through the terrible early days, and the hard, demanding, co-operative labour to rebuild modern civilization.
Then, of course, the sobering fact comes out that it would cost billions of dollars, perhaps an average of $4 billion for some years. I think this is perhaps a cost which the Canadian people are unwilling to accept. It is not going to be politically popular. However, other nations have done this. Sweden has built public shelters for its people. It is argued that these are the same things which the United States is doing. We accept this argument, and it has a telling effect. But I am sure if the Americans are going to be decimated, that is no argument that the Canadian people should also be destroyed. We know the extent of the fall-out that has occurred so far from tests that have been conducted. If an anti-missile missile is developed in the next few years, surely the explosion which will take place over Canada as we defend against this attack will create fall-out.
What I always have in mind, as do these authorities to which I have referred, is that we have to deal with the future. Even if the Minister of National Defence is right in saying that only a small percentage of the megaton load which the Russians have can be effectively used against us, that may not be the case over the years from now on. Surely it is not wise to tell Canadians to build $500 shelters which might be completely useless by 1965 or 1966. Assuming we have a population of 18 million and that an average of 3 or 4 people use each shelter, we are asking the Canadian people to spend between $2 billion and $3 billion of their own money on measures which may not offer them adequate protection. People should have some right to hope that survival is possible under these conditions.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that the years to come might well be years of sacrifice and austerity. Perhaps this is an area where we shall need to make sacrifices in future, as well as in connection with the Department of National Defence itself. I must say that my views have definitely changed on this subject. At one time I looked upon shelters as a colossal waste of time; I felt that a nuclear war would cause such tremendous devastation that shelters of any kind1 would be irrelevant. However, I now think we have a duty to civilization, a duty

to humanity, to ensure the survival of some percentage of the population.
I agree with the Prime Minister in his statement that efforts must be made to make sure the government carries on. However, I think the people of Canada are somewhat concerned that we may be more interested in ensuring the survival of the upper levels of government than we are in the welfare of the average man. I know that some years ago the story was that we should never have another war because it would mean that those who started it would die in it. Now the people are losing that feeling of confidence. They are no longer confident that the people in the top echelons of government are as concerned about the people at the bottom as they are about themselves.
We can reach a decision with regard to building public shelters. The cost will be fantastic, but surely we must be realistic about the nature of the threat and the cost of meeting it. We may disagree with many of the things which Bertrand Russell says and does, but there is one statement he made with which I am sure we all agree, namely the statement that since Adam and Eve ate the apple, man has never refrained from any folly of which he was capable. I believe we must make some kind of response to the threat which faces us. However, both the threat and the nature of our response must be assessed realistically and the public must be enabled to look upon the emergency measures organization as an organization sincerely determined to ensure their survival.

In the course of a statement dealing with the emergency measures organization, as reported on page 8293 of Hansard for September 13, the Prime Minister advised the house that in planning for the survival of our people accurate public information was of vital importance.
With that statement I agree completely. There is, however, one facet of educating the public on which I should like to speak briefly. From conversations with some of my constituents I have the impression that among the majority of men there is a growing awareness of the need to learn all we can about the consequences of a nuclear war. However, in the case of some women-and I emphasize the word "some"-there seems to be a defeatist attitude which leads them to throw up their hands in despair and say there is no point in preparing shelters because if even one nuclear bomb were to drop on us there would be nothing left.
Possibly women look at the problem of survival in a different light from men. Consciously or unconsciously a woman's thoughts and actions are directed at perpetuating the human race, and unless she can see some

security for her family she may feel that there is no point in even trying to survive. In parades and demonstrations against the nuclear bomb and the building of shelters the majority of those who take part are women and children; at least this has been the case in all the demonstrations which I have witnessed in Vancouver.
We can understand the horror with which women, particularly, regard a nuclear war, but I suggest that the government must impress upon all of us that we have a duty to survive. It makes no difference if nine tenths of the population are wiped out. It makes no difference that the country may be completely devastated. Those who remain must carry on. They owe it to themselves as human beings and as citizens of this country to do so. God forbid that we should have a nuclear war, but if there is to be that possibility each one of us must prepare ourselves for that awful event. Once we admit the danger, we can devote our energies and resources to meet that crisis, instead of wasting our time wringing our hands in despair.
I knows as well as anyone what could happen in the event of a nuclear war, because I attended the one month survival course at the civil defence college at Arn-prior, and I believe I am the only member of parliament to have done so. Having attended that course I am less afraid of the consequences of a nuclear war, because I know what to do in an emergency and I am much more confident of my own chances of survival. No matter how huge the loss or how great the suffering, we must go on. And without the women of our country, Mr. Chairman, there would be very little reason for us to survive.
Supply-Privy Council at any time suggest that I am an expert on the feelings of all men with regard to this or any other problem.

On a question of privilege, may I remind the hon. lady that I referred to "some" women and emphasized the word "some". If I can undertake to speak only for some women, does the hon. member for Niagara Falls imply she speaks for all men?

I can only undertake to speak for those who sent me to parliament, and I am not always sure I am able to do that.
With regard to this matter, I have had correspondence from many individuals, and most of the authors happen to be women. They are, of course, the people most concerned. They are the cradle of civilization, as they have been in the past. They are particularly concerned, because they feel this is a problem which is more likely to affect them since they will be remaining at home during the day and during the evenings. They are concerned not only for their own children but for the children of all mothers all across the world.
It is because of this concern that such groups as the Voice of Women have arisen across Canada. This is not a left wing organization, though the hon. member for Vancou-ver-Kingsway referred to it as being such in a debate a week or so ago.

May I
inform the hon. lady that I never made any such a statement in the house. I read a statement from a publication which made that claim. I never made any such statement personally.
I hope that in the months ahead the government will develop a program which will help those women who now hold the conviction that there is no purpose in learning how to survive, to believe once again that there is still very much to live for, and that by taking a few precautions they can, in the absence of a direct hit, ensure their own survival.

I had hoped to make a few remarks with respect to this subject. Although the situation was well covered by the statement made on behalf of this party by the hon. member for Essex East there are certain observations I wish to make, particularly in the presence of the Prime Minister. I am glad to hear that the last speaker is an expert on the feelings of women in connection with this and other matters. Despite the fact that I am a woman I do not 90205-6-554i

Well, the hon. member read it with apparent approval, and it has caused concern to many of the members of that organization, which is not and has never been considered a left wing organization. The article read by the hon. member was one which referred to them, but it does not convey the impression which he may have erroneously left.
This is the reason organizations such as the Voice of Women are springing up. It is felt that women outside of public life, who constitute at least half of our population, can actually participate in shaping the future of the world. They are not a lot of wild-eyed, pie in the sky people; they are responsible people who care, and I suggest that this is the sort of movement which elected representatives should be pleased to see becoming established.
Here we have interested citizens who are coming forward to assist their elected representatives. Further than that, organized

Supply-Privy Council groups of women and women throughout the country of course are greatly concerned. They have listened to and read with great care the statements of the Prime Minister within the last few weeks on the proposals which this government is going to undertake to assist in the survival of the people of Canada. But to those in Niagara Falls, and indeed, to those in Ottawa and in other major centres, that is in what are called the 16 target areas-I do not know whether these are in fact in the 16 target areas, but many newspaper reports in the past have indicated that Niagara Falls is listed as one of the primary Canadian targets-the Prime Minister's proposals seem far fetched with respect to the protection and assistance which will be given to the people of Canada.
In his statement the Prime Minister mentioned that a prototype bomb shelter was to be built. This is the first reference that I have been able to find to a bomb shelter. My understanding is that in case of a direct hit from a nuclear bomb it is unlikely that anything would give adequate protection unless it was something of the type of shelter which is being set up to ensure the continuation of government. Certainly nothing which an individual could hope to build would be sufficient against a direct attack.
In many reports, and particularly in one by Dr. Edward Teller, to which the hon. member for Peterborough referred, which was widely circulated through the offices of the Associated Press, it is said that one third of the American people-and I imagine this figure would apply to Canada-could be protected well enough by fall-out shelters. Dr. Teller went on to say that one third would be in trouble, but they could have a 70 per cent chance of survival if given decent shelters. I assume that these people would require bomb shelters. Then he went on to say:
One third of our people would not even he In danger, because they don't live near targets the bombs hit.
The Minister of National Defence told us it was likely that only one or two bombers would get through. If any bombs were dropped on Canada they would be intended for the 16 target areas, and some concern should be directed toward those target areas.
they were asked where they were from. When the man who was in charge was told they were from Niagara Falls he took away the pamphlets and said, "These are of no use to you; you are in a target area." They came to me as their representative and said, "What are you and what is the government doing with respect to those of us in a target area. Are we in those 16 centres across Canada to be completely abandoned?" I was unable to give them any answer.
There are many in the fringe areas, who by no stretch of the imagination would expect to be struck by a bomb, who have considerable apathy about building even a fall-out shelter.
I think it represents more of fear than of apathy. They do not like to hear discussions, and they feel there is really no reason to do anything because, as many women say, "Why should I come up? My husband might be gone, my children might be gone. I would not want to survive in what was left of the world.
Women have a great deal of resilience and courage. In past wars they have been shown to be as strong as or stronger than the men who stood or fell at their sides. Even though they express those opinions they will get out and try to do something to protect their children. But this is the sort of letter I have been receiving, and I should like the Prime Minister and those responsible for the emergency measures organization to consider it. This is a letter from a woman in Niagara Falls. It says:
But even if my neighbours and I had basements and could afford to build shelters, it still wouldn't help our families. Take mine for instance. Three of my children are in school. They attend three different and widely separated schools. The youngest is seven. His school, which is nearest to home, is a good 25 minutes walk from our house. There are no nearby fall-out shelters to which they could run-there is no protection whatsoever for our school children. A nation's future is its children. In a nuclear war Canada's future will be wiped out. My husband is in construction work. To what public shelter could he and his fellow workmen run? In the meantime, I am to sit home in my (theoretical) fall-out shelter for two weeks and go quietly mad, knowing all of my family and most of my neighbours are surely dead.
In letters to the press this same feeling has been expressed again and again; would it be worth while to survive if everyone that
I am asked by my constituents what is their position. I should like to tell the Prime Minister that two women from my area went to the Canadian national exhibition this fall to see what might be done with respect to fall-out shelters, and they went with the derision of their husbands and their neighbours ringing in their ears. They spent the afternoon there and obtained all the brochures and information. As they were about to leave
one holds dear cannot survive? Even those who would wish to provide themselves with shelters of one kind or another have this problem, and I quote from two letters which I found in the letters to the editor column of the Toronto Star. I substitute the word "government" for what is here:
Will government please tell a $50 a week truck driver from Cabbagetown-

May I tell those who are not familiar with the Toronto area that that is what they mean.
-with a wife and two kids and $22 a week rent where to pick up $1,200 for a shelter? Maybe we should try a finance company.
In the other letter from Trenton we find the following:
I make $65 a week and have a wife and seven children. A dollar down and a dollar a week is our speed, and X don't think Khrushchev will give us the time.
These are the people who care, the people who wish to do something. I would say they are the people who deserve to be assisted. If governmental assistance is to be provided for those in non-target areas for a fall-out survival shelter, more must be done to assist than merely to provide assistance for a loan, and something important must be done with respect to those in target areas. If there are evacuation schemes, and they are feasible within a possible 20 minute warning, are they known to the municipalities and the people concerned?
According to press reports the Clerk of the Privy Council and indeed the Prime Minister are building fall-out shelters. There have been press reports that these two gentlemen will not be in Ottawa. Are they to be prewarned of any sort of attack upon Ottawa? If so, I assume that their shelters must be built either as an incentive to show the people the way, while they know they will not have to use them, or they are built to provide what shelter they can for those of their dependents who will be left behind.
I am not sure whether Ottawa is a target area, but I would assume that it might very well be. If it is a target area, I ask this question. Is the provision which they are making for their dependents going to be in any way adequate? I ask them to consider the plight of those hundreds of thousands of people in the most heavily concentrated areas of our population in Canada, those people where there is a heavy concentration of secondary industry, of power development, of rail or other transportation facilities; those people who will be the first to die in Canada should the bombs drop and who now, before they die, cry out to the government for support, for aid, for a plan for evacuation.

Mr. Chairman, the voices of members of parliament today are music to my ears, because I have been talking about civil defence since 1958. Therefore I will be very brief. I am happy to say that it feels much better not to be a lone voice in the house. I want to recall some of the words of Sir John Hodsoll, co-ordinator of civil defence for NATO, who visited Canada in 1955. I
Supply-Privy Council
believe he stated that any bombers that may be shot down over this country will at the same time set off thermonuclear bombs.
As a matter of fact it may be safer if one lives in a target area, provided our defences are good because this means that the bombers will fall on other areas, but any bombs or missiles carried by these bombers will create dangers for all those in the area where the bomber or missile is shot down. The more effective our defence, the more dangerous it will be for Canadians generally at any point in Canada. Canada will likely be the battlefield in the next war, and we will have to take the brunt of a thermonuclear attack. If our southern friends are capable of shooting down these bombers all over Canada, Canada will be hit by all these bombs and Canada will be the most dangerous place in the whole world.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this debate has been of considerable interest to me, because on the occasion of exercise Tocsin early this summer I had the responsibility of being the federal government representative in the province of Ontario. I can report to hon. members that in my opinion the exercise was a first class course of instruction in the type of co-operation that can be achieved among different levels of government in working to achieve a common purpose. The participation by both federal and provincial officials in the exercise was of the greatest use in indicating to them at governmental level the responsibilities that would be theirs and the way in which those responsibilities could be carried out.
I must express at this time my appreciation of the participation of Premier Frost and his cabinet, most of whom were present at the provincial headquarters at Camp Borden, as well as my appreciation of the participation of the large number of provincial members who showed interest. After all, this is one matter in which the provinces must indicate a continuing interest because it deals with the fundamental area of property and civil rights, damage to property and the survival of the person in the form of the individual.
I was also most interested in the split speech of the hon. member for Peterborough. When he first spoke on September 13 I was ready to excuse some of his remarks because I thought he might have entered the debate on the spur of the moment and might not have had a chance to carefully examine the letter to which he referred. However, I thought that between then and now he would have availed himself of the expert opinion that can be had before putting on the record a letter that is incomplete and before accepting the statements contained in that letter and

Supply-Privy Council endeavouring to attack a responsible program without first having availed himself of the information that is at hand.
I should like to deal with Dr. Whittier's letter as I heard the hon. member read it, and some very significant omissions. In his letter Dr. Whittier criticizes the pamphlet "Eleven Steps to Survival" and says that a basement fall-out shelter is only 90 per cent effective whereas the pamphlet indicates that such a shelter is 99 per cent effective. What the doctor and the hon. member have omitted to indicate is that the reference is to a basement shelter, that the protection afforded by the house itself is equivalent to 10 per cent, and as 10 per cent of 90 is 9 you therefore arrive at 99 per cent.
The same thing applies to all the other arguments advanced by way of criticism of this type of shelter. The letter refers to radiation areas equivalent to direct blast, not to such areas as those for which the fall-out shelter suggested by the emergency measures organization is designed. This shelter is designed to deal with the fall-out to which it is anticipated that Canadians would be subjected in the unlikely event that there was ever an atomic explosion in this, or a neighbouring country. The hon. member has completely overlooked these things. I draw to the attention of the pedagogue from Peterborough that one of the rules of pedagogy is that you know your facts. In this instance the hon. member has completely failed to substantiate the letter he received. Perhaps he was overly impressed with the degree the doctor holds and did not go into the merits to see whether the criticism advanced by the doctor is warranted.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say I have checked some of these facts with other physicists who have experience in this field. Furthermore, he is dealing with fall-out shelters not in a blast area. As far as blast is concerned, we all know that these basement shelters are of no use whatsoever, so I think the hon. member should be fair.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
I am endeavouring to be fair, and I point out to the hon. member that he was dealing with fall-out in a blast area where the concentration is the highest. The hon. member will have an opportunity to speak again. Surely he does not suggest that everywhere in Canada the degree of fall-out suggested by Dr. Whittier is going to take place. If he does, then he just does not have any conception of what is going on, and I suggest that he devote himself to attentive reading of the material that is available to find out what is going on in this particular field. The $500 basement shelter to which he


refers provides an opportunity for the individual to survive, and after all we are talking about the survival of the individual. As a socialist he does not understand individuals.
I was rather surprised at the remarks of the hon. member for Niagara Falls, who talked about central survival systems. Man's basic philosophy is his own survival and the survival of those who are dependent on him. This is a method by which under fall-out such as is anticipated the individual man and his family, if they are home at the time anything happens, can have the assurance of some protection. This is an effort that the individual himself can make. The cost is an estimate. A man can do it himself and it will not cost nearly $500. If he wants to call in a first class contractor then it will cost that much. This is a constructive and forward step taken by this government to aid an individual in doing what he can to help himself, in taking those steps which are necessary to protect himself and his family from fall-out that may result in the unlikely event that an atomic explosion ever takes place in this country.
The hon. member for Peterborough, in what I might term his multibarrelled peashooter criticism, endeavoured to bring the Associate Minister of National Defence into this debate by referring to his suggestion that limited war was unlikely. The hon. member denied, therefore, the very principle of the N.D.P. or, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate terms it, the S.O.P., that there will not be an atomic war. The hon. member should be consistent, but perhaps it is not within the realm of possibility for him to be consistent. If they are right in their defence policy, in which they say there will not be an atomic war and no steps should be taken to deal with an atomic war, then he should not get up in this house and try to alarm the Canadian people by saying there is going to be massive obliteration by atomic bombs of this country. In doing so he surrenders completely his responsibility as a member of this house. The speech which he made was self-contradictory of the views of the party to which he professes to belong.
Since hon. members are criticizing the things we are doing in this country. I would refer them to the September 25, 1961 issue of U.S. News. I do not know whether this is where the hon. member obtained his information about Dr. Teller's views, but they are mentioned here. What are other countries doing in this respect? I quote:
Japan, the only country that actually has experienced atomic bombing, has no national plans for defending her people in a nuclear war ...
The British show less concern than Americans about the danger of a nuclear attack. Britain's

civil defence corps is dying on its feet because the government has not been able to get enough people seriously interested in It...
French optimism: Nuclear bomb shelters are practically unheard of in France. A French official says: "Most people here think nuclear war is unbelievable."
West Germans show no interest in building bomb shelters ...
In Belgium, Holland, Sweden and Italy you find the same story-nobody building shelters for a nuclear attack.
In Sweden there are all kinds of shelters.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
The hon. member will have his opportunity to speak. These are responsible statements made about the other western countries which are not advancing at the same rate as Canada with respect to civil defence. We know what we are doing in this country with respect to civil defence measures.
The hon. member for St. Boniface indicated that in the event bombers were shot down, there would be atomic explosions as a result. I can tell him that my information is quite to the contrary; these bombs will not explode. There have been instances, as we know, in the United States where bombers have actually crash landed and the bombs have not exploded.

May I ask a question?
Mr. Pallet!: I know the hon. member is an expert in this field and has made a lengthy study of these questions. The technical information leads us to believe that the bombs would not explode unless they had been activated and that, of course, would be highly unlikely in the event a missile or bomber were shot down.
This is a good program for individual participation. It is a program that needs the assistance of the members of this house because it deals with the survival of a man, his wife and his family. It is disconcerting to have a member stand up and criticize, without foundation, a program that is designed to help a man and his family. The hon. member for Niagara Falls mentioned the Voice of Women, an organization is this country. I refer her to the most recent Russian news letter, which says that the Russian women are in full support of the Russian atomic explosions. This is something that should be brought to her attention.
Why contrast the two. That is unfair to Canadian women.

I point out to the hon. member that I am not offering any criticism of the Voice of Women. I am merely pointing out, since she mentioned their name, that the voice of Russian women is in support of atomic testing in Russia.
It is just about one o'clock and I should like to conclude, if I may. This is a program for the individual who can, with his own hands, achieve some measure of protection against the fall-out dangers inherent in an atomic explosion.
What about the children in school; what can they do?

This is absolute nonsense, but may I call it one o'clock?

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

At the outset, Mr. Chairman, I must say that I listened with a good deal of amazement to the oratorical outburst of the hon. member who spoke previously. I refer to the hon. member for Peel. In this item in the estimates of the privy council we have before us one of the utmost importance and one which must be considered, in the light of its presentation, the allocation of money and the statements made by the Prime Minister and others, as one that is

Supply-Privy Council
being considered on the basis of national survival in the event of an all-out nuclear war which we hope and pray will never occur. I was therefore not only amazed but surprised and disappointed by the attitude taken by the hon. member for Peel. As far as I am concerned, I can only interpret his speech as being one made from the position of an apologist of government policy and proposals on expenditure, as one put up as a sharpshooter endeavouring to shoot down members who take this matter seriously and who want to ask serious questions and to get constructive answers. In other words, it could only leave with me the impression, on the basis of what he said, that the government policy and proposal is paper talk and poppycock and that basically what we in this House of Commons and the people have received up until now is propaganda oratory.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: No; that is not right.

The minister will have his chance just as I am having mine. The reason I say that in particular is to be found in the opening remarks of the hon. member for Peel when, in substantiation of his support of the government's approach, proposals and policies on national survival, civil defence, or call it what you will, he based his experience-and these were his opening remarks-on what he had seen and what he had knowledge of from having had the opportunity of taking part in exercise TOCSIN.
The Prime Minister did as I think he should have done with regard to exercise TOCSIN. He announced it in the House of Commons. He told us that it was to be a realistic exercise in facing the problems of nuclear attack against Canada, with bombs falling on Canada, in order to demonstrate just what could be done on a dominion-provincial basis to carry on the functions of government in Canada. The Prime Minister was good enough to invite two members of the opposition to take part in exercise TOCSIN-and I want to thank him for the invitation-and to be among those evacuated from Ottawa to Petawawa. I was one of those who were invited and I went all through that exercise. It is because of what I saw and because I was given the right and opportunity to ask questions and get answers-and here again I wish to thank the Prime Minister-that I am speaking now. I say very seriously that we must consider just what are government policy and proposals for survival, especially in view of-and I am coming back to the hon. member for Peel- what I saw on exercise TOCSIN, which was a federal exercise from Ottawa to Petawawa,

designed to carry on the operations of government, carry on communications with all the provinces, to maintain the economy as best we could and to provide for the defence of Canada. May I very briefly run through that experience which was a practical one or a tactical one, as we were told by the Prime Minister.
First of all, a train must be on 20 minutes call at all times-and it was there-in order to move the government or the ministers, their deputies and the administrative heads, the chief personnel of the army and the civil service, to the only underground shelter we have and which is located at Petawawa. It takes a couple of hours to get up to Petawawa. I imagine anyone who is going to attack Canada will have saboteurs here. At least I imagine they would do so. First, may I say that there was no security check whatsoever. I never saw anybody challenged.
They saw you coming.

Then I am glad they understood my loyalty and my patriotism and recognized me. However, I saw many whom I did not recognize and I never saw them being checked. I know the premier was not there. That was very unfortunate, because he died at five o'clock in the afternoon.
Which premier?
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, we may say many things about the Prime Minister, but it would be unfair to say that was true.
Mr. Chairman, I am not quite sure what the hon. member said. Did he say it was unfortunate?
No.

I did not think so. However, according to exercise TOCSIN, Ottawa was wiped out shortly after five o'clock that afternoon; and you, sir, had stayed in Ottawa. There you have this practical, tactical exercise on survival conducted by the federal government, with all these civil and governmental operations.
During the time spent between Ottawa and Petawawa, no communications were kept on the train. So if you had been there, sir, according to this tactical exercise all your heads of government, your chiefs of staff, your ministers, your deputy ministers and your chief personnel would have been completely out of touch with what was happening in Canada during that period.
This was a tactical, practical exercise, so I asked where the communications were kept on the train. The answer was that they did not know whether they had any, but they most likely had. The government wanted

to keep down the expense of this exercise and that is why there was no communications system.
We arrived in Petawawa. There we were immediately told what the situation was, and of course your cabinet, sir, and everybody else would have been completely out of touch during the time it took to travel from Ottawa to Petawawa. We were briefed on the situation. Then we were taken around and shown all the administrative set-up. Then we received the warning that just outside Petawawa there had been an atomic explosion so we had time, because it takes a little while for the radiation to come down, to go underground. This tactical, practical exercise was truly an experience. The chief personnel of the federal government, sir, your chiefs of staff, your heads of police were all there and in all probability would have had to stay there for up to 2J weeks because this explosion was just outside Petawawa.
What did we find? We learned at about 10 minutes after five o'clock I think it was-I may be a little bit out in the time-from the teletype underground that Ottawa had been bombed. If I remember correctly, there were
60,000	dead and I do not know how many injured. But Ottawa was out. Underground in Petawawa there was the administrative control of all Canada, and nearly all of them came from Ottawa. I asked one question immediately, "Ottawa is out?", and the answer was, "Yes". I asked, "What is the reaction of all these people here? Their wives, husbands, children, sweethearts and parents are all dead". This information had just come over the teletype. The answer I received was, "Well, they are just carrying on with their work". Like the blazes they would carry on with their work, if that was the real situation. I asked what was the situation to take care of the psychological factor involved in what had occurred. I was told that this had not yet been considered.
If this had been a real attack, sir, these people would probably have had to remain underground for up to 2J weeks, if there were radiation outside. I asked, "That is why you are here, and you are not going to open the doors. Where are you going to put your dead?" I was shown a refrigerator which would hold one corpse.
Did you try it for size?
There was just this one refrigerator. I am being very serious, sir. This was the TOCSIN exercise as I saw it.
Don't be ridiculous.

I am not being ridiculous; I am telling the committee what I saw. In this situation communications all across Canada

Supply-Privy Council would be of the utmost importance. We were shown over all the communications system. They were proud of their system and they had reason to be. But this they did tell us, Mr. Prime Minister, that it was not the latest, most up-to-date, efficient equipment.
Moreover, all the communications mechanism and teletypes were underground, but the actual dispatch system was above ground. This was an old building that had been converted for this purpose. There may be some other building under construction at the moment and I understand there is, but I am talking about the TOCSIN exercise which was carried out, and the government of Canada would have to continue.
If there were any leakage of radiation it would be in the corridors, and people would have to live for a long time in the offices and rooms. However, that aspect of the matter had not been planned very well. There was air conditioning in every office and every room, and all the air was filtered. But there were no tight doors, so there was ventilation that could not be shut out by closed doors. Therefore it was the same as being wide open, and these people could not have been protected in any way in the event of radiation escaping into the building. It cannot be said that this is ridiculous. The hon. member was talking about exercise TOCSIN. This is what I saw in the exercise. These are the questions we asked. This is the type of planning and engineering carried out by the government. This is how the money would be spent.
Perhaps more important than that is this matter. I do not think we have yet heard any statement from the Prime Minister or others in the government about this. I wonder whether or not since TOCSIN No. 1 the government has been able to work out the relationship with other governmental jurisdictions so that in the event of attack and national survival operations being put into immediate effect government could be carried on.
Let us not forget this. In this house we have listened on many occasions to speeches on constitutional jurisdiction, jurisprudence, control and matters of that sort. The hon. member for Peel was the federal co-ordinator, I believe, in Manitoba.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Peel is in Ontario.
I know, but I thought the hon. member was the federal co-ordinator in Manitoba. During the TOCSIN exercise I asked what was the actual statutory authority of a federal co-ordinator.

The War Measures Act.

Supply-Privy Council

I asked whether the authority was clear under the War Measures Act. I was told that they thought it was. A message came in from all the provinces on the devastation which occurred according to this exercise, and they needed, I think it was 15,000 men to be moved from one area to another. I asked the question, "Where is the statutory authority when a person is endangered by being moved to an area of devastation?" While I was there, over the teletype came a request for the movement of 12,000 workers from one area to another. This I can tell the Prime Minister. The answer I got when I asked that question was, "That is a problem and we are working on it".
I should like to know whether or not that problem has been worked out? I am only telling the committee what I was told. They said they thought it would require legislation of the House of Commons. I think we should know these things because these are the types of questions that were asked on that TOCSIN exercise in which we were invited to take part by the Prime Minister. These are the things we saw; we just did not hear about them. I am not talking about something I have read in the newspapers; I am talking about something I saw, and I only saw it because of the courtesy of the Prime Minister in allowing us to go on that trip. These are some of the answers I received to the questions I asked. I think we are entitled to more detailed information about the program, about the policy and its effectiveness.
I think the hon. member for Peel made the most serious mistake of his life when he criticized what was said by the hon. member for Peterborough, who was only asking the government to face reality and answer some of the questions which are in the minds of some of the people of this country. It is not good enough to tell the people in a blatant manner what they should do. The average individual in Canada is not in a position to build a shelter. I represent a strictly working class constituency-a heavily populated constituency in the middle of Vancouver. I imagine this would be a target area, so-called, in the event of an attack. Very few of the people who live there could afford to build a shelter which might cost between $500 and $900. Moreover, the majority of the people who live in my area do not own their own homes. They rent their accommodation, and the average man is not going to spend upwards of $500 building a shelter in a home he rents-a home in which he may not be living in a year's time. I have yet to hear of one landlord who will put one in.

I think we have to face this situation. In addition, we may as well stop this stupid saying that the position today is better than it was in past years. Every well informed writer I have read on this subject says that any war which starts out as a conventional war is likely to develop into a nuclear war, and this means a nuclear war without restriction. This leads us to the marvellous phrase used by the Prime Minister-"coexistence or nonexistence". The item we are now discussing is provision for the event that we may have to face the possibility of non-existence. From what the hon. member for Peel outlined, I cannot see this government, its ministers or their deputies continuing to exist in the event of an atomic attack, judging by what I saw in Petawawa, if that is to be their protection. That was a tactical exercise, I believe, and I think I am correct in saying that when it was over there were only 11 members of the House of Commons still alive. I never did find out whether that would mean I would have any spot in the administration, but that is by the way. These are serious matters and we approach them in a constructive manner. I am confident at any rate, that the people do not want any shilly-shallying. They are prepared to hear and discuss hard facts. They want to know whether there is any possibility of survival in the event of a nuclear attack on Canada. If there is, they want to know what is to be done and how they can do it as individuals. I believe that the individuals in Canada cannot do it. I doubt whether even Canada as a nation can do it with a population spread over 2,700 miles and up to the Arctic circle. We are asking not for bombast but for realism, honesty and frankness in dealing with the public so that they may have a better understanding of the picture. Though I have no authority for saying this I have no hesitation in telling the committee that if we could get a practical program, the money to operate it and the means to operate it in the event of a world catastrophe which we all hope will never come about, then the Prime Minister would receive the wholehearted support of members of this group because we want to see people live and not be evaporated, as was mentioned by a great speaker in England, in the event of a world holocaust of nuclear death.

This morning I made a quotation from memory concerning the danger from bombers or missiles which might be stopped by our own military defences. I mentioned Wing Commander Sir John Hodsoll, chief civil defence adviser to NATO.
I should have mentioned Dr. Alvin C. Graves, scientific adviser to the Nevada test site operations, Los Alamos, New Mexico.

On August 1, 1955, this is what Dr. Graves said while addressing a convention of mayors and representatives of municipalities:
People in Canada have a problem which is somewhat different from the problems of the people in the United States. The reason for that is the geometry of the earth and the line-up of the powers of the earth today. The reason is that if an aircraft were dispatched to attack the United States under present circumstances we would expect it to come over the North Pole of the earth down from the Arctic regions and down through the plains or the mountains or eastern portion of Canada, attack some targets in Canada, attack many targets in the United States. The plan would be to try to shoot as many of these planes down as possible.
I would like to say one thing, though. When those airplanes are shot down they will carry with them the atomic bombs or thermo-nuclear bombs with which they were dispatched. What of these weapons? Will they crash to the ground and do nothing? I cannot answer that question since I do not know the Russian plan, but it is perfectly possible to put a mechanism on an atomic or thermonuclear bomb such that it will detonate when it drops below a certain altitude. It is perfectly possible to provide that it will detonate when it strikes the ground.
I think we would be more than foolish if we did not at least assume that the Russians might do that.
Those are not my words. They are the words of an expert telling Canada and Canadians what to expect. I know the hon. member for Peel has explained that full protection will be provided against atomic explosions in the event of accidents in peacetime to planes carrying nuclear weapons. However, the Russians, sending over planes or missiles to bomb targets in North America, would not want to waste their bombs; they would want them to explode no matter where they might fall.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver Centre on the wonderful address he gave this morning. I should like to congratulate him on being the only member of the house to take the civil defence course at Arnprior. I know that if the people of Canada were properly trained and taught how to safeguard themselves against danger they could face an emergency without panic. They would be able to do the normal things when this emergency would begin. I suggest that no school teacher should be given a degree or permit until he had taken a civil defence course and that no school student should be given a certificate of promotion until he or she had taken such a course. I think that is the place to start-in the schools. Let us train all our children. We hope the danger will not come soon, but it may. Let us not wait until those students have become adults. They should receive full training with the least expense. Teachers might be given an extra allowance by the government in order to take the training. They should be paid an allowance for teaching these extra subjects 90205-6-555J
Supply-Privy Council in the schools. These things are being done elsewhere. I suggest this is the time to start.
