speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was very interested to note the reaction of the hon. member for Peterborough and the hon. member for Vancouver East to the government's proposals in the field of civil defence. The Prime Minister is to be congratulated on stimulating these two members to take the interest they have shown in recent days in this problem. They are almost rebels, Mr. Chairman. They are unique in the party or parties to which they belong. I think I can say something about this. I was the federal commissioner for Saskatchewan during exercise TOCSIN, and one of the things that impressed itself on my mind at that time was the lack of seriousness which the C.C.F. government of Saskatchewan showed with respect to that exercise and the little regard that the provincial premier and the members of his cabinet paid to the safety of the people of their province as evidenced by their co-operation in that exercise. The lack of co-operation was manifest. There was not a single cabinet minister from the province of Saskatchewan who took part in that exercise, not one. Not one even had the courtesy to come to civil defence headquarters to take part in it, although we had nine representatives from junior positions in the provincial civil service.
To demonstrate the intense interest of the C.C.F. in saving the people of Saskatchewan in the event of nuclear war we might examine the contribution they made to that exercise in the field of medical component, the medical side, where surely I would think that if that government were going to take the exercise seriously they would see that there would be adequate medical components represented there; but there was not one from the province, not one single representative of the provincial medical staff or the provincial health services.
Another example of the active interest of that government in saving the people in the event of nuclear attack was the interest evidenced in regard to the problem of transportation which inevitably would become a problem. Roads have to be kept clear and maintained. There has to be transportation for different facilities of rescue, survival, food and so on. Therefore one would imagine there would be a large provincial component in the field of transportation in such an exercise, particularly when the provincial government owns the bus lines in that province. What was the provincial representation from Saskatchewan in regard to transportation in the field of bus, road or air transportation? It was nil. They could not turn a wheel, my friend from Provencher says. The contribution of the only elected C.C.F. government in
8796	HOUSE OF
Supply-Privy Council the history of this country was practically nil. The regard in which they held this problem was less than nil.
If the two members who have spoken from that corner, the hon. member for Vancouver East and the hon. member from Peterborough, could form themselves into a committee of two to wait upon the leader of their party, the present premier of Saskatchewan, and give him the benefit of their ideas and suggestions in this particular field, they might stimulate his interest and show him that rebels in the new party might be successful in their attempts to draw the attention of that party to the vital things which affect the Canadian people.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to prolong this debate, but I do wish to answer one or two remarks made by the hon. member for Peel. I am not going to say anything about the speech which preceded his. Of course, in relation to other provinces I should like to know just what is taking place in each area. Of course I do not agree with what the hon. member for Peel suggested. He said that nothing constructive had been said because no one mentioned the measures which the Prime Minister referred to. Nobody suggested that less money should be appropriated. What we are concerned about is that so far the ordinary emergency measures have not made a very good effect upon the people of Canada.
This afternoon some 60 members are sitting in this chamber. They have a better opportunity to know what is going on than any other group in Canada. I wonder how many in this chamber have built a fall-out shelter in their basements, what percentage would there be. This is a rather interesting question to ask, and it would also be interesting to get some statistics on it. This is the problem we are trying to deal with. We do not think this has yet made any impact on the people of Canada. This is why we are taking an active part in this debate.
The hon. member for Peel suggested that the remarks I made this morning dealt with fall-out in blast areas. Well, of course, the hon. member knows, or at least he should know, that there may be no fall-out at all in the blast area. Climatic conditions may cause fall-out away from the blast area. It might be swept into other areas by the prevailing winds and very little fall in the blast area.
We seem to be in complete disagreement as to how much fall-out there might be. The hon. member for Peel says, "we believe it would be a certain amount". On what basis does he arrive at this conclusion. I realize he may have privileged documents at his disposal which are not available to the rest


of us, but nevertheless this is a question on which we will never know who is right; at least we do not want to know on the basis on which we can find out.
He turned on a member of his own party who was trying to explain this morning just how serious the situation is. The hon. member for Peel made a passing reference to the socialists and said we evidently do not believe in the liberty of individuals. With
323,000	people unemployed and all their dependents, with some 400,000 people unemployed recently and all of their dependents, and with the possibility of many thousands in farm communities making less than $2,000 a year, would it not be a difficult problem for them to get this much money together? The hon. member for Peel and his party say that they are for individual enterprise. Certainly this does not apply only to the wealthy. I should hope not. Surely this does not mean every man for himself, or, as our leader put it, as the elephant said when he danced among the chickens. I am sure he did not mean it that way.
I have only one or two more points to make. The hon. member also referred to the voice of women. I am sure he will correct himself in this regard. He referred to them in the same breath as the women in the U.S.S.R. who had made some statements about nuclear testing. I am sure he is not attempting to link these two situations and bring into disrepute an organization which is asking questions, perhaps embarrassing questions, but necessary ones.
Finally he suggested that there is a great difference between our attitude on survival and that of the officers of this particular political party. Our survival policy is very simple. It is based on the fact that a war may start, and no one in Canada can make that decision because we will not have the weapons to make such a decision. It can happen by accident. We recognize that is the situation just as I am sure the Prime Minister does. That is the basis of our survival policy.
On the other hand, our defence policy is that we do not want Canada to encourage such a war to take place. That is the basis of oui refusal to accept nuclear weapons. I can assure you that we in this group are seeking to find the answers to survival. We do not believe we have the answers. We do not believe that the government really thinks that it has all the answers. We are trying to ask questions and put forward proposals in a constructive way, and I hope that in future our position will be clear.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the discussion on this subject. What I have to say will be

said with a full realization of the difficulty involved in trying to plan for an adequate program to protect our people in the event of a nuclear war. In my opinion this subject is too important to permit us to be involved in digressions that are not directly related to a solution of the problem.
I think this is perhaps the most difficult problem facing any government in any country of the world at this time. I say that not only because of what I have listened to today and what I have read, but also because at one time, I had a responsibility in connection with this matter. Anyone who has had that responsibility will appreciate that the problem is indeed a gigantic one. This does not mean that we should not put forward ideas in discussing the present government's program with a view to improving that program. If that is done it should not be thought that we are engaging in idle criticism. Certainly that is not what I rose to do at this time.
I am not fully convinced that the problem of leadership in this matter, which is essential, is one that can most effectively be met by the ministerial division that exists at present. I am not asserting this dogmatically. But when the Prime Minister announced a year or two ago that the responsibility for civil defence would be divided between the privy council office, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Justice I wondered if such a division of responsibility was the wisest course. I do not suggest that there is not a function for all of these departments, and, even for other departments, to discharge. But it seems to me that the over-all direction of civil defence requires constant attention to the problem in its full context.
The Prime Minister, it is true, when questioned about this by me at the time, did say that direction would be given by all four ministers, but that we could look to the Minister of National Defence as die one to whom questions should normally be directed. I took it from that and from something that General Pearkes later said that General Pearkes would be regarded as the minister in the government at that time who might be looked upon as the spokesman for the government with respect to matters having general application to the problem of civil defence, but that this did not preclude the Prime Minister from dealing with the estimates now before us. The Prime Minister is a busy man. It would seem to me that it would be difficult for him to give the kind of over-all attention which I believe is required. However, I may
Supply-Privy Council be wrong in this. Perhaps the Prime Minister will comment on this point when the moment for doing so arrives.
I recognize, of course, that in the privy council office, under the Prime Minister, are individuals who for a long time have been interested in this problem, and who had experience in certain aspects of civil defence before their transfer to the privy council office. I know from personal experience that the Clerk of the Privy Council has always had an intelligent and deep interest in this problem. He is responsible for the war book, and I am sure that the Prime Minister and those associated with him have had much to do with the program involved in E.M.O. with regard to such things as providing for the transfer of government and the like.
The hon. member for Peel spoke today and I do not think he did full justice to himself or to the cause which he was seeking to champion. It is not a question whether this government is doing more than any other government in the western world. It is not a question whether, in the light of greater knowledge and greater tension, the government is doing more in this field than its predecessor. We are not going to resolve this question by seeking to engage in that kind of argumentation.
The hon. gentleman spoke of the shelter program and said that the general directions given by the government were not fully appreciated by some hon. members, who had participated in the debate, because they had failed to recognize that this program was one directed toward individual participation. If by that the hon. gentleman meant that we cannot have a successful civil defence effort unless every individual citizen takes an interest, then I fully agree with that characterization by the hon. member for Peel. Obviously if the people of Coventry do not want to provide for their defence in the event of a nuclear war, no effort on the part of the government or on the part of their fellow citizens is going to provide the necessary defence.
In that sense what the hon. gentleman said is correct. But if by individual participation he meant that the whole problem, say in the matter of shelters, was to be left to the individual, then I believe the hon. member has not fully stated the case. I am sure it is not the intention of the government, or of any government which directs itself to this problem, that the civil defence organization is to be predicated upon exclusive individual participation. If that were the case, we would not be concerned with the building up of supplies, the storage of medical supplies, preparations for the storage of food, the building

Supply-Privy Council of emergency hospitals and the like. There is a very wide area of collective effort without which there can be no successful civil defence effort.
Just as that is the case, so too is it that in a country like our own the job cannot be done only by the federal government. There must be the fullest co-operation at all levels by all governments, provincial governments, municipal governments, supplemented by voluntary organizations, the Red Cross, the St. John Ambulance, all of them together providing a collective effort on the part of the citizens and the community as a whole. So that in that sense what the hon. gentleman for Peel said is not correct.
He was greatly in error, of course, when he spoke about shelters and what was being done in other countries. If I understood him correctly, he said, for instance, that in Sweden no shelters were being built. Well, that is not the case. Not only are individual shelters being built in Sweden but the state has built all kinds of shelters, and this they have been doing for some time. In fairness to the situation in the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada, I may say that the provocation for Sweden to engage in a large program of public shelter construction is much greater or was much greater than in the case of those countries with which I have just compared Sweden. The fact is that Sweden has built underground shelters, taking advantage of their great rock formations, large shelters where not only can people go for refuge, security and safety, but shelters where there are actually large industrial establishments and the like. So that in Sweden, contiguous as it is to the Soviet union and with the provocation that exists, there is a wide program of public shelters as well as individual construction of these devices to minimize the effects of blast or fall-out.
Now, the government is wise in giving direction in the presentation of prototypes of shelters. It is wise in bringing the pamphlets up to date and indicating there is a great deal that can be done by the individual to protect himself against nuclear war. I completely subscribe to the view of the Prime Minister that whatever may be the cataclysmic destructive consequences of nuclear war, there is much that can be done to save percentages of our population in the event of a nuclear war. There is much that can be done, and it is a policy of defeat on the part of anyone to take any other view. Certainly, it is not strengthening the deterrent to say that all we have to do is sit back and take whatever is levelled against us by a would-be aggressor. There is a great deal that can be done. That is why the government


of this country, and other countries, must at this time be supported in the efforts they are making to try to give the necessary direction.
I know that this is not an easy problem by any means. What are we to do? The government has said shelters can be built and these shelters can provide a great measure of security and resistance to blast and fall-out. But the government has not, I realize the difficulty, indicated if the time has arrived or whether in the future it will be proper to give consideration to much wider participation by the state itself in the construction of shelters. I have read the interesting speech made by the hon. member for Trinity who participated in this debate following the statement made by the Prime Minister on September 13. The government has not stated unequivocally if it is prepared to embark on the kind of program that has been embarked on by Sweden, for instance.
Has the government reached a decision yet as to whether or not the federal government and provincial governments together, or with the municipalities, should begin to build public shelters? Now, that is the great issue which I believe is being discussed at the moment and being canvassed in our country. Are we to leave this responsibility to build shelters exclusively to the individuals, to the fathers and mothers of families, or are we to supplement private construction for individual family purposes by a contribution from the state to build a shelter in the individual home which will serve undoubtedly the purpose intended if the construction follows the recommended line? However, this is not going to provide all the shelter that will be needed in the event of nuclear war. Supposing a nuclear war takes place during school hours. The children are not going to be at home, they are going to be in school. Are we going to provide shelters for these thousands of children in the schools. Most of our working population will not be at home during certain hours of the day. They will not be able to rush from the factory or the office to take shelter in the family basement. They will require shelter forthwith at their place of work.
Unless the government builds shelters, the only way they can be provided will be for industry to build them, or the office people in a building to collectively get together and build a shelter, or the individuals in a school to collectively pool their resources to build a school shelter. These are the problems about which we have not yet had a decision and in connection with which there has not been any declaration of government policy. The cost of building shelters on the scale that I have been envisaging is tremendous. I noted that the hon. member for Trinity mentioned

a figure of $4 billion. He may be right in his estimate, but I have seen a much higher figure. It is the responsibility of the government to decide, in the light of all our obligations, what should be done in this regard.
The government is in a better position now to determine the likelihood of war. We were all encouraged by the statement of the Prime Minister the other day when he did not believe we would have what the newspapers call in their headlines, a hot war. With the information that is at his disposal, this is a heartening statement. He will have to determine, as head of the government, whether or not that situation may deteriorate, whether or not with the expansion of the ownership of nuclear weapons to other countries than those now in possession of these instruments of destruction, the danger of miscalculation or of accident will become increasingly great. He will have to assess the consequences of such development.
I simply say, speaking for myself, that I believe it is the duty of each and every member of parliament, as I am sure all of us recognize, to support the administration in the effort it is making. We have a responsibility also to indicate what we believe are the areas in which decisions have yet to be made. I believe it is not unfair to suggest that the government should announce its policy in that context or indicate why it does not feel at this time it has to go farther than it has gone.
Now, these general remarks will be interpreted in various ways, I suppose, by various people, but I have stated my views as I conscientiously see them. However, I make them in the full sense of an effort to try to contribute to the solution of what I know to be an extremely difficult problem.
My final comment is this, I believe the hon. member for Peel did an injustice to some of the women of our country when he spoke just before noon. He contrasted the views of the women of the Soviet union as expressed in a document that came before him today with some Canadian women. The women who have organized themselves into the Voice of Women or "La voix des Femmes" are, as far as I can tell, an organization of women who firmly believe, as do we all, in peace. They believe that it is up to each individual person to make a contribution and not to leave that responsibility to the government only. I think it would be wrong to suggest that they are not motivated by the best of intentions, particularly when one bears in mind the fact that this organization is sponsored by some very eminent women indeed in our own country and in the world. For instance, among them 1 find the name of Senator Josie D. Quart of Quebec city, a
Supply-Privy Council woman who has devoted much effort to promoting the United Nations society. Then I notice the name of Mrs. Roosevelt, the wife of a former president of the United States, a woman who has done so much for the United Nations and for good international relations. I also find the name of Mrs. Pearson, the wife of the Leader of the Opposition and other names I do not recognize. They are the names of women who in their own country are distinguished and who have made great contributions. I notice the name of Mrs. Adelaide Sinclair, formerly of the Department of National Health and Welfare, now the director general of the children's committee with headquarters at the United Nations. She is one of our most distinguished women and is certainly associated with women who can be in no way regarded as having produced evidence of having a lesser interest in our welfare than have any of us. Then I notice the name of Mrs. Wendell Willkie, the wife of a former candidate for the presidency of the United States. I note that the chairman is Miss Muriel W. Jacobson. Miss Jacobson was national director of the Canadian committee for world refugee year in 1959-60. From 1952 to 1957, she headed the voluntary international assistance unit in UNESCO's New York office in the United Nations. I believe she is now corresponding in Canada for the United Nations high commissioner for refugees. I do not know Miss Jacobson and I do not know all the women whose names I have mentioned, nor have I mentioned other women who are on the board of directors. I know little about the organization. However, I know of the contribution made by these women to our national life. I believe that they are sincere women who believe that only by mobilizing public opinion can they support a government in its declared policy of peace and goodwill.

I shall be very brief in taking part in this debate. There is certainly no need in urging on anyone a strong civil defence program for this country. That is generally being agreed upon by those who have taken part in the debate. However, for any civil defence program to succeed, it must be accepted by the public and be supported by every person in the country. I therefore think it is most important that we stress the positive values of a civil defence program.
Most of those who have spoken have indicated that we are living in a dangerous world and that, whatever may be our efforts at the United Nations and elsewhere to maintain peace in the world, there is always the risk of nuclear war, and that if we are going
8800	HOUSE OF
Supply-Privy Council to survive we must have fall-out shelters and a civil defence program in this country. However, I think that the possibilities of civil defence go beyond that. In fact, in the years ahead the program of civil defence might well be the main determinant as to whether or not nuclear war comes about, when we consider the position in which we find ourselves today, with each side trying to threaten the other with nuclear weapons and in actual fact holding the people of each country as hostages in order to prevent that war coming about. However, we realize that situation is brought about only because each side is afraid that in the event of nuclear war its population would be destroyed. That is the theory of the deterrent that we have been a party to. However, when you consider the possibility of one side having a very strong civil defence and being able to remove their population from the position of hostages, it certainly would put the other side in a much stronger position. Hence we can see that if the Soviet union were to go on a massive program of civil defence and place themselves in a position in which their population could be protected whereas the population in the western world were vulnerable to a nuclear attack, we would be placing ourselves in a very dangerous position. If it were the intention of the Soviet union to bring about a nuclear war then, of course, that situation could only encourage them to do so.
I therefore think there is a positive value, a deterrent value in civil defence which is just as important as is the deterrent value of our nuclear weapons. I think that this aspect should be stressed throughout the country and be pointed out to the people of the country. As I say, if that aspect is not made clear and if the people do not understand the importance of civil defence, it is very hard to gain public acceptance of such a program. There is no doubt that there has been reluctance on the part of the public to enter wholeheartedly into civil defence, because generally speaking we have considered nuclear war to be unthinkable. It is only recently that the situation has come about where we have had to face that possibility. Particularly when the stress has been laid on the fact that we must have fall-out shelters to protect us in the case of attack, I think the public have been reluctant to accept the program entirely on that basis. I think the more positive aspect is the part that a proper civil defence program can play in preserving peace and avoiding a nuclear war. This aspect should be very well to the front of any program that we put forward to stress the importance of civil defence in this country.

First, I wish to say that it has been most helpful to have the expression of views of hon. members on this matter. What was said a moment ago by the hon. member for Essex East was true in every respect, namely that this is a matter that requires the best thinking not only of the government and the parliament of Canada but of the provincial governments and the municipalities, as its success depends on the co-operation of each and all. I was interested in what the hon. member for Vancouver East had to say. He said it in turgid words. He described what took place on the occasion of the last exercise. It has always been the policy to have an unprejudiced and unbiased person such as he on an exercise like this, in order to have the benefit of such views as the hon. member expressed regarding an exercise that is part of the survival plan and as such transcends any party considerations.
The hon. member mentioned the need of full liaison between federal, provincial and municipal governments and, while maintaining the constitutional separations of authority, to bring them together in days of peace so that if war should come the plan would have been completed and in effect.
I would say that exercise was a helpful one. It revealed how things would be in actual operation. The hon. member mentioned that he travelled by train and that no security precautions were taken. I can assure him that everybody knew him and such precaution was entirely unnecessary, as it was with the others who boarded that train that day. If he has any idea that he travelled to Petawawa without being identified by the security authorities, I can assure him, that is not a fact.
The hon. member pointed out that authorities there advised him that the signal equipment was not the most modern. That was so. More modern signal equipment had already been ordered and some has been delivered. The rest is generally ready. This was an exercise.
When the hon. member speaks in connection with the disposal of the dead, I can only say that his views are not accepted by those who had the responsibility of bringing together the organization that met in Petawawa. That is not to say that all was perfect. Far from it. That is the reason hon. members from all parts of the house were given the opportunity to be present. All of us are in this together, and by giving this opportunity to those who have different political viewpoints than the government we are assured that a fair measure of criticism will be made. Such criticism is necessary if this difficult problem is to be met, because we are in an

experimental position. As one hon. member said, we will only know it it works should the eventuality take place that all of us are guarding against. We are trying to do what can be done now to meet the exigencies of the future by co-operation between the various departments of government.
I am going to refer to what the hon. member for Essex East had to say about organization and the division of responsibility among various departments of government. This was an action taken following the fullest study of what was being done in other parts of the world. I believe we have reason to have a feeling of pride in having brought about the division in question, for only in recent months the United States adopted a system almost analogous with many of those things that we undertook experimentally. They have seen what our action has been and have concluded that this is the action they should undertake, and they are doing so now.
These exercises have to take place from time to time. A few weeks ago I advised the house that a further exercise had been decided upon. The government has decided that because of the current international tension and the necessity for checking the state of readiness in respect to a civil emergency, a national civil defence exercise shall be held late in October or early in November. It has now been decided that this exercise will take place on November 13, extending so far as participation by governments is concerned into November 14. This exercise follows naturally from the one held in May, 1961, in which I frankly admitted to the house certain gaps had become evident, which I believe have been remedied in the meantime as a result of that previous exercise.
It will be our endeavour in arranging this exercise that as many as possible of the Canadian public will directly participate and to a greater extent than was the case previously. With this in mind, a good deal of public information will be made available both before and during the exercise. Extensive use will be made of radio. People will be asked to listen to the broadcasts and to review the plans they have made for the safety of themselves and their families. It is hoped that full support to the exercise will be given by provincial and municipal authorities, whose responsibilities in the event of war are of major importance.
With this in mind I have written the premiers of all the provinces, inviting them to have their governments participate in the exercise and to encourage various municipalities in each of their provinces to do likewise. I would stress that this is a further step
Supply-Privy Council in a series of tests to review how ready we are to meet the grave emergencies and dangerous implications that will arise in case we are involved in war.
There is no way in peacetime that this can be done excepting by way of an exercise such as the one we held in May and the further one to which I have alluded. I agree with those who say it is difficult to command and mobilize the public interest in this matter. One hon. member mentioned the fact that I stated the other day that I could not believe it possible that there would be war. By that I meant that I could not conceive that any national leader, whether it be Khrushchev or anybody else, knowing the potentialities of nuclear war and possessing ordinary human intelligence, would wish for war or dare to make a direct move in that regard. But we said the same about Hitler, and it has been said of all the leaders of mankind who have become military megalomaniacs, that they would not go to the limit of war. In the past they have, and in the past, too, there were great fears. Those fears are with us today. Fearful as I am as to what would happen should a nuclear war come, I am not one of those who believe that mankind would be destroyed. I believe that philosophy was built up by Nevil Shute in his book and has caused the hearts of men to be more fearful than the facts of science would justify.
Certainly, the loss would be terrible. It has been estimated that in our own country if a series of nuclear attacks were made upon us the number of casualties would run between two million and six million, which is terrible however one views it. That is why our efforts are directed to bringing about peace, and that is why every waking minute and every waking year all those who have responsibilities have before them that picture of the awfulness, of the havoc of the future, and also of the need to do everything, to preserve peace, consistent with the maintenance of those things which are dearer than life itself.
When organizations spring up for the purpose of doing their part I welcome them. Any group of men and women who join together and endeavour to mobilize opinion within their country on behalf of the best things of life are performing a service; I recognize that as good citizenship. I listened today to what the hon. member for Peel said and also to those who followed him. I think they have done him a grave injustice in the interpretation they have endeavoured to place on his words. He spoke of this organization in Canada and the ideals for which it stood. Then he said that in the U.S.S.R., on the other hand, the women there were standing firmly behind the need for the maintenance and use of nuclear power. He was showing
8802	HOUSE OF
Supply-Privy Council the distinction between those who stand for peace and those who in the U.S.S.R. become automata under the control of the state, carrying out the will of the state. We need to mobilize public thinking with regard to the precautionary measures that must be taken in order to maintain the safety of the individual in Canada. It is hard to do. We are all built the same way. Everyone says in his own heart: it just cannot be-something will turn up to prevent the outbreak of hostilities. Therefore we need the help of members of parliament and of all in public life to mobilize the thinking of Canadians to the need of acting, and acting now, to do those things necessary to provide and assure a reasonably high figure of survival. I am going to say a personal word in that regard.
As Prime Minister my responsibility is provided for in the division of powers between the various ministers. I believe in the need for a shelter program. I am entirely convinced that there is much merit in the basement fall-out program which has been placed before the Canadian people. I know there are some who leave the suggestion that we have in mind the survival of some and have not the regard for others that we should. This was implicit in certain words spoken here which I am not going to identify, although the hon. member in question will, no doubt, know of whom I am speaking. That is a principle which all of us cannot but condemn; we cannot but condemn any effort to leave the people of Canada with the view that we seek to protect those who are rich and not those who are poor. It is the responsibility of government to ensure a reasonable equality in this regard and that is one of the things which is before us at all times.
The hon. member for Essex East pointed out the tremendous cost of a national shelter program. The cost is, indeed, fabulous. All of us who have taken the time to read the information brought together by those responsible for the administration of E.M.O., know that there are vast problems in this connection which have yet not been solved here or in any other country.
I was going to say a personal word. As Prime Minister, I occupy a house on Sussex street. It was suggested to me that we should have a shelter there-a shelter really protective to the "nth" degree. That is where I shall be when and if war should come. That is where I shall stay, and we have there now a basement shelter identical with the one we have asked Canadians to put in their own homes. There is not one bit of difference between that and the one we suggest for others, excepting that this is to accommodate the staff as well as my wife and myself; it covers those in the building. That is where


we shall be. That is the understanding, and that understanding will be carried out. I want that realized across this country-that there are no protective measures being taken for the survival of any particular person in this country.
There are, however, responsibilities which rest on a government to ensure a continuance of government, for, without government and with a completely separated group of ministers, you would have chaos. To that end we have available for the purpose of ensuring the continuance of government, for the cabinet, senior civil service officials and others needed to maintain the organization of the country, protection similar to that which has been provided in other countries.
Hon. members may say to me: what will the basement shelter protect against? Well, it will not protect against a direct hit or anything like a direct hit. The only kind of shelter which would protect from that would1 be a shelter one thousand feet down in rock. What we are trying to protect against are the major dangers we face, that is, from drift, from fall-out and the after-effects from radiation. I think the hon. member for Vancouver Centre made a particularly good contribution to the debate today when he emphasized the need of educating the people about this and showing them that what we are trying to do represents the considered opinion not only of the government but of all the officials and also of experts in other countries who have been consulted regarding the course we should take.
I mentioned a moment ago that we have to interest people. The hon. member for Essex East said that he had occupied a position of responsibility and he realized some of the difficulties. I shall point out some of the increases in expenditures that have taken place and of the action taken by this government as danger has become more and more imminent internationally with the passing years. In 1952 and 1953 the program was initiated of sharing expenditures. The amount expended was $1,400,000. The federal allocation to the provinces was based on 8 cents per capita plus an additional 6 cents per capita in designated target areas. Cost sharing was on the basis of 50-50 between the federal government and the provinces. In 1954-55 the appropriation was $2 million and there was a slightly higher per capita grant to the provinces, namely 11 cents per capita plus an additional 9 cents per capita in designated target areas. In cost sharing there were three alternative amounts, as follows: first, 25 per cent municipalities, 25 per cent provinces and 50 per cent federal; second, 75 per

cent municipal and 25 per cent federal; and lastly 50 per cent federal and 50 per cent provincial.
In 1957-58 cost sharing was still 50-50 as between the municipalities and the provinces on the one hand and the federal government on the other. The amount of the appropriation was $2 million.
In 1959-60 the appropriation was $4 million. As of April 1, 1959, we made provision under treasury board minute to provide more generous contributions. The federal allocation was based on a 25 cent per capita grant. Cost sharing was 75 per cent federal, with a 25 per cent share by the provinces and the municipalities, with a further provision that if any portion of $4 million remained after provincial and municipal projects submitted by May 1, 1960 had been approved and committed, further commitments could be made to the extent of the balance. In 1961-62 the appropriation is $4,350,000, and the federal allocation is the same as that in 1960-61.
This does not begin to show the total amount of the expenditure by the federal government on civil defence. That is an amount, including expenditures in the armed forces, of some $44 million.
With respect to the number of people participating, I cannot give the committee figures in detail in recent months, but the figure as of December, 1960, shows that over 100,000 volunteers and 187,000 full-time provincial and municipal employees could be engaged. Of these about 96,800 have received some training in their emergency duties.
In connection with the emergency measures being taken, all ten provinces and a total of 308 municipalities are participating. It should be noted that, depending on the province, a municipality might be a county, which means in effect over 1,200 municipalities are actually engaged in emergency measures activities.
In so far as federal expenditures are concerned, they have continued to increase. I refer particularly to grants to provinces and municipalities for civil defence and related purposes. Between 1952-53 and 1956-57 they ranged from $246,000 to $813,000, in round figures. They have increased since from $972,000 in 1957-58 to $2,245,000 last year. It is estimated that this year it will be about $3,700,000.
Mention was made by the hon. member for Essex East of the delegation and distribution of authority. I should like to refer now to what President Kennedy has done in this connection. The executive order regarding civil defence was made in the United States on July 20. The delegation of authority to
Supply-Privy Council the secretary of defence by President Kennedy assigned to the secretary of defence certain civil defence responsibilities, among others, a fall-out shelter program; the warning system; emergency communications including warning and monitoring; emergency assistance to state and local governments in a post-attack period; protection and emergency operational capability of state and local governments; and programs for financial contributions to the states for civil defence purposes.
The order reconstituted the former office of civil and defence mobilization into a new agency known as the office of emergency planning to give advice and assistance to the president in determining policy, appropriate defence roles; helping the states to enter into interstate civil defence compacts and the like.
It will be noted that the main assignments to the secretary of defence under this executive order are most similar to those assignments to the Department of National Defence in Canada by order in council in 1959. The new office of emergency planning in the United States is quite comparable with the emergency measures organization set up in Canada in 1957.
The hon. member for Vancouver East asked under what authority we would act in the event of hostilities. I mentioned the War Measures Act. During exercise TOCSIN we went through the formality of having a cabinet meeting for the purpose of bringing in the War Measures Act-the document was marked as being a defence exercise-so that we would be able to do the things to which reference was made by him and in particular the transfer, I think he said, of some
15,000	people from one area to another.
As the hon. gentleman knows, when the War Measures Act is promulgated the federal parliament and government become almost supreme, particularly in the field of legislative power, and are enabled to do those things which otherwise, under the heading of property and civil rights, would fall exclusively within the jurisdiction of the provinces.
I should like to refer to a question raised by the hon. member for Essex East and I think also by the hon. member for St. Boniface, who has devoted himself very greatly to this problem and was, as he described himself, in this regard a lone voice in the wilderness for a considerable period of time. The question was raised as to what should be done with respect to the schools. A strong case can be made out for the provision by school authorities of fall-out shelters in schools. This problem, however, like all the

Supply-Privy Council others to which the hon. member for Essex East referred, is tremendous in its implications. Children are actually at school only about 20 per cent of their time during a day and by far the greater part of their time is spent at home or near home. Therefore on the basis of priorities, and I think the provinces take this view, a stronger case is made for the provision of shelters in their own homes. Even in the 20 per cent of time that they are at school it is generally felt, having regard to what may be expected as the normal warning time, that they would have sufficient time to get home. However, as time goes on the case for fall-out shelters in schools to take care of the one chance in five that the children will be there when the attack comes becomes stronger. Nevertheless, starting with fundamentals I think our number one responsibility at the moment is home shelters.
Mention was made by an hon. member of target areas and what can be done in a nuclear attack to safeguard people who live in target areas. That is a problem that has not been solved by any government in any part of the world. If one is immediately under a bomb there is nothing that can be done. If the weapon is somewhat farther away blast-proof shelters are of some help but they are tremendously expensive.
We have distributed to those who have asked for them plans for a blast-proof shelter that can be built in one's yard and there are also plans available for groups or communities that may wish to undertake such shelters. Incidentally, I wish to refer to the very patriotic offer that has been made by the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada and the institute of professional engineers. Representatives of these two organizations called upon me yesterday and offered to the government and the country in the interests of Canada as a whole their services and those of their membership. They promised to do whatever they can and whatever they are asked to do not in a spirit of monetary gain for professional services rendered but rather to show their interest in national survival and in the need of co-operation on the part of Canadians as a whole. The staff of the emergency measures organization is working on a cheaper form of blast-proof shelter based on using heavy steel tanks such as those used in gasoline service stations. The government has suggested to municipalities that they should have plans ready that will make it possible for those people who wish to leave target areas to do so if they so desire, always depending on whether there is adequate warning time before the explosion.
It is not recommended that all people leave such areas because there are serious conflicting considerations that arise. If the warning


time is very short it is not possible to leave at all. If one is out on the roads it is even more dangerous than taking cover in the basement of a house closer to the blast. Mass evacuation suggests itself to many as a simple means of meeting the problem but it contains serious risks of panic. There is no doubt that if the problem permitted and arrangements were made to allow a substantial number of people to leave, many thousands of people could save their lives by moving out of the most dangerous areas; but to do so they must have places to go to. They run the risk of going to some place where they are exposed to the weather and possibly the danger of fall-out radiation. For this reason the general feeling is that people should only try to move out provided they have some place to go and know of it in advance. Instructions to this effect have been given and I think they are a matter of public record.
The suggestion has been raised that the government should build blast shelters. This could not be done on a partial basis and something of the immensity of the problem was indicated by a number of hon. members. It would mean that we would have to provide for some five million to seven million people. So far as that decision is concerned, I ask you to place yourselves in the position of the Prime Minister. If we proceed with such a policy costing at least a billion dollars, some say several billions, and war does not come we will then be subject to widespread condemnation for improvident action. We have been inclined to take the stand that that is one risk we have to take, that our purpose is to save the lives of as many Canadians as possible and to see that saving those lives shall not be based on the possession or lack of possession by people of the necessary wherewithal to protect themselves.

Would the right hon. gentleman permit a question at that point? I wish to thank the Prime Minister for his candor in referring to target areas. Because I have seen two lists in different press reports, I would ask the Prime Minister to put on record those areas in Canada designated as primary targets by the emergency measures organization.

I think there is no reason why that should not be done. Without designating actual areas I would say that if a nuclear attack on North America were to include a direct attack on Canada, major cities, industrial centres, ports and seats of government such as Calgary, Edmonton, Halifax, Hamilton, London, Montreal, Niagara Falls, Ottawa, Quebec City, St. John's, Newfoundland, Saint John, New Brunswick,

Toronto, Windsor, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Victoria could be considered as the most likely target areas.
The hon. member for Peterborough produced a letter from a Mr. Whittier. The gentleman in question wrote to the emergency measures organization expressing his views and we welcome such co-operation. I think, however, that there were some errors in the representations made which were based not on a lack of technical training but on a lack of the full knowledge of all the circumstances. The hon. member said that the correspondent stated that on page 10 of the booklet, "Eleven Steps to Survival", it is implied that the fall-out comes from activation of earth, stones, buildings, etc. but that the booklet goes on to give the decay rate for fission products arising from the fission of U-235. These statements are not inconsistent. Actually, what occurs is that the material blown up is made radioactive by the adhesion of radioactive fission product dust particles. Therefore, it is quite proper to say that the rate of decay as applied to the fission products from the fission of U-235, may be used in describing the rate of decay of the fall-out; and this is fairly applied independently of the land area over which the detonation occurs.
I think the explanation will be understood by all hon. members. With respect to the next point raised by the correspondent in the excerpt by the hon. member, it is apparent that there has been a misunderstanding on his part. It is true, as he suggests, that the shelter described in "Blueprint for Survival No. 1", of itself will stop 90 per cent of the radiation present. What has been overlooked is the fact that this structure is placed in the basement of a house. The hon. member for Peel dealt with this particular phase of the letter. In such case, the house itself will have at least a protective factor of 10. This means that the end result of the basement shelter in most houses is that the protective factor is 100 instead of 10 and that 99 per cent of the radiation, instead of 90 per cent, is taken care of.
I think there were a number of other statements in his letter, and I think they were answered in the reply which was sent to the correspondent of the hon. gentleman. If I have omitted any, it has not been from lack of a desire to meet the points raised but rather from the fact that I have not got the particulars before me.
Now, sir, mention was made of civil defence planning for cities. The federal government can plan for nuclear war as it will affect larger cities only in a general way, since circumstances vary so much. However, it can, with the provinces, help the cities in their planning and it has done so in many
Supply-Privy Council ways, namely, by providing a guide for municipal planning which has been widely circulated; by providing courses of instruction for mayors, other municipally elected persons and for civic officials; by providing financial assistance toward costs that arise in connection with local planning. The federal government pays 75 per cent of the costs of approved planning projects, as I mentioned earlier. Planning in detail, however, is the responsibility of the city in question and many of the cities in Canada have developed their plans fairly adequately.
I think that, in general, covers the matters that were raised. Again may I say how indebted I am to all who have made a contribution. We want the very best ideas that you have and that Canadians as a whole have in this regard. In concluding, I am again asking for the fullest co-operation. We have entered a field of activity that is novel; we have entered one that is dependent upon the uncertainties of the future. However, I have this to say regarding Mr. Curry and Mr. Bryce, of the privy council, as well as the administrative staff and the various staffs in the provinces, they have done a great deal and gone far beyond the normal call of duty in order to make a success of dealing with a problem which is novel, unusual, but vital to the future of the people of our country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the Prime Minister could bring us up to date in connection with the position of this commission. The Prime Minister will recall that I asked him on the orders of the day when the second volume of the report would be ready. He told me he had a memorandum from the Clerk of the Privy Council. I should like to know now, having regard to what the Prime Minister indicated on a number of occasions, what the position is and what progress has been made by this royal commission.

I stated the other day that the second report would be available this fall and that there would be a third report as well. This latter report would be a compendium of the working papers and the statistical information that had been gathered and collated by the commission.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Prime Minister will remember that in the first report which was

Supply-Privy Council tabled there were a number of recommendations made costing, I believe, somewhere in the neighbourhood of $100 million. The recommendations were divided into four different categories. The Prime Minister will remember that there was a discussion of this matter on an earlier occasion and he indicated that as soon as the report was brought down legislation would be forthcoming. I should like to know what the intention of the government is with regard to the recommendations of the MacPherson commission and whether or not any of those recommendations are going to be implemented by legislation.

As the hon. gentleman knows volume I dealt with more or less general matters and had some recommendations. It is necessary for us to have volume II before us before we can finally determine several matters that were recommended and in respect of which further information will be forthcoming in the subsequent volume.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
There are a number of other things upon which I should like some information. The Prime Minister will remember that the object of this royal commission was to consider a number of matters incidental to transportation including, amongst other things, freight rates and the freight rates structure. The point on which I should like to make inquiry at this time has to do with vote 317 which is now under consideration and is related to vote 590. Vote 590 concerns the $50 million which we will be asked to vote under the heading of "Board of Transport Commissioners".
As the committee knows the Freight Rates Reduction Act provided a sum of money, which I believe was in the amount of $20 million, for the general reduction of class rates across Canada and that money has, I take it, been paid by the government to the various railways since the bill was given royal assent. Can the Prime Minister tell the committee whether or not any part of this $50 million will be paid also in reduction of freight rates or how it will be paid?

I have not that information and when we come to the $50-million item no doubt there will be a discussion. I think it would be well to have the facts fully before us rather than endeavour to answer the question piecemeal.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Well, I will not insist on it, Mr. Chairman. I think perhaps that answer is one which would commend itself to the committee. Then dealing with the royal commission, may I ask this question. Can the Prime Minister tell us when it is expected that the final report will be brought down?

He will remember that when this matter was discussed in the house, he was under the impression that this was something which could be done very quickly. As a result of our experience as members of the former government, we indicated that it took quite a long time, as has been the case. Can the Prime Minister give any indication of when the final reports will be given to the house?

If I could do so, I should be most happy to be of assistance in that regard. I remember one time when I entered into the field of royal commission prophecy. Events did not bear me out, and from time to time questions were asked. I do not wish to be placed in that position again.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Clark report.

The hon. gentleman is like Orpheus. He could almost get information on any subject when he takes the kindly attitude. However, I am not going to enter that field even in the face of the blandishments by means of which he has endeavoured to secure the information.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Prime Minister is in very good humour.

In the same mood and with the same purpose may I ask the Prime Minister if he can now tell us when the government expects to be in a position to announce its policy of acceptance or rejection, in whole or in part, of the Bladen commission report? The Prime Minister will appreciate the fact that this is a matter of great interest to the community from which I come. The report has now been in the hands of the government for some five months. There is considerable interest in knowing when we may expect something in connection with this matter.
The hon. gentleman, too, almost persuaded me, Mr. Chairman. However, I cannot add anything to what I have already said, even though I am so highly desirous of being helpful.

318. Expenses of the royal commission on government organization including the payment, notwithstanding the Civil Service Act, of honoraria or allowances as may be authorized by the treasury board to officers, clerks or employees permanently employed in the civil service for services rendered by them to the commission, $750,000.

I am not going to make the mistake made by my colleagues of asking the Prime Minister to prophesy. I am simply going to ask the Prime Minister to tell us what has been accomplished or to give us a report on what has already been accomplished by the Glassco commission and particularly

to give us the most up to date estimate of how much of the half billion dollars this commission was expected to save has been saved by it.

May I say to the hon. gentleman that the commission has undertaken an extremely large and comprehensive examination of the problems that were placed before it. It divided its inquiry into 18 specific projects. I ought to place those projects on record to give an indication of the comprehensive investigation taking place. They are as follows: Financial control and accounting; manpower in the government service; paper work and office systems; real property management; procurement and materials management; transportation; communications; economic analysis and statistics; legal services and procedures; scientific research and development; services to the public; medical and hospital services; education services; public information services; lending, guaranteeing and insurance activities; administrative aspects of the Department of National Defence; government operations in competition with private business; federal-provincial joint and allied activities.
I am sure that enumeration will give the committee some idea of the complex and wide ranging field in which the commission is operating. It does not hold public hearings. It has endeavoured, as far as possible, to secure its information by consultation with departments of government and outside.
As to the savings it will bring about, may I say that I hope that it will be able, without in any way diminishing efficiency but rather indeed increasing it, to recommend changes which will assure reductions proportionately similar to those achieved by the Hoover commission in the United States.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I take it that this is the first time an estimate appears in connection with the Glassco commission?
Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is for $750,000?
Yes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder whether the Prime Minister can tell us what the total cost of this commission will be? I hold in my hand an article which was published in the Financial Post of July 29, 1961 and in which it is stated that the cost of this commission for this fiscal year will be about $2,250,000. Can the Prime Minister say whether or not that is a fact?

I know that, when you have some regard to the nature of the expert information that must be secured, the cost will be considerable. I would not be able to
Supply-Privy Council give an estimate at all at this time. However, to make it an effective commission, the personnel must be those with wide experience and knowledge, technical, economic and the like. Whatever the cost may be, I think the results will be far in excess of it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That remains to be seen. We shall be obliged to await the recommendations of the commission. Can the Prime Minister give some indication of whether this commission will, in connection with this report, proceed along the same lines as those followed by the MacPherson commission, for instance? Will there be an interim report or will there be a number of interim reports?
As the hon. gentleman knows there has already been one interim report. There should be another one in due course.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When is it expected that this commission will finish its work?

As the hon. gentleman knows, when the commission was set up the purpose or objectives were set out and it was provided that the commissioners should report to the governor in council, making interim reports on the progress made, the final report to be made within a period of two years.

I have not the documents before me at the moment, I admit, but at the time the commission was appointed I seem to recollect that it was stated that it would make reports from time to time and that it would also make recommendations to government departments in the course of this operation, with a view to having them implemented immediately, in order to effect as quickly as possible these economies which, after all, as I understand it, are the sole purpose of the commission. I wondered whether the Prime Minister could give us some indication of the number of recommendations and of the nature of the more important recommendations that have so far been made to the various government departments by the commission in the course of its operation.
I have not that information, Mr. Chairman.

I do not wish to hold up the estimates. I wonder whether the Prime Minister could have the information prepared in some sort of form that could be made available to hon. members within a reasonable time, so that at least it would be available for consideration at the next session of parliament.

I will give consideration to that request.

Supply-Privy Council

Mr. Chairman, there is another suggestion that I might make to the Prime Minister about this royal commission, in which it will be understood that because of my previous experience in the public service I take a special interest.
Have you given any evidence yet to the Glassco commission?
I understood the Prime Minister to say that the commission was not taking evidence.
By that I mean recommendations.

As I understand it, it is carrying on a sort of inquisition in private and not a public inquiry; a sort of star chamber, to use a phrase that was very frequently used by a very distinguished member of the house who used to sit on this side of the chamber and is now sitting over there. So far I have not appeared before this august body during its inquiries, though I must say, since the Prime Minister has put the direct question to me, that some legal officer connected with it did telephone me the other day and suggested he would like to talk to me about something. I offered to take him to lunch so that he could do so. I hasten to add, that was to be at my own expense, not wishing to add to the cost of the inquiry.
What I particularly wanted to suggest to the Prime Minister was this. I noticed when the Prime Minister was reading the various branches of the inquiry that one of them was for public information. The Prime Minister will recall that when he sat on this side of the chamber some years ago the critics on this side of the chamber-I do not know that the Prime Minister indulged in this very much, but the Minister of Finance certainly did, and some of the leading members of the opposition who are now on the treasury benches-complained about the excessive cost of public relations officers and information officers in the various branches of government.
In view of the importance which hon. gentlemen used to attach to this subject I was wondering whether the Prime Minister could suggest to Mr. Glassco that this particular branch of the inquiry be expedited and that an effort be made to make a report on this subject in as public a form as possible at the earliest possible date. I ask this because I can well remember how the Minister of Finance, in particular, used to point out what a tremendous saving could be made by reducing these services.
The only clear and precise recollection I have is that before 1957 and right back to

confederation, as far as I know, there were no public relations men in the Department of Finance, and the only economy that has been effected so far in this particular department has been to add someone at a reputed salary of $10,000 a year to the staff of the Minister of Finance.
Knowing the passion for economy of the Minister of Finance, who has not increased the annual expenditures of this country by much-over a billion dollars a year from what they were when the previous government was in office-I think that an area where it was recognized these great economies could be made ought to be explored as quickly as possible.

speechtext: are still outstanding may be dealt with agreeably at the next session of the house. However, up to this point this is the progress which has been made and I hope, now, that the committee will give its approval to these estimates or, if there is some matter which hon. members feel should be dealt with, that they will bring it to my attention.

I should like to thank the minister for the statement he has just made and also for his kind remarks about the efforts and the work of the parliamentary committee on veterans affairs.
As the minister has pointed out, these estimates were examined very thoroughly in committee. In fact, ten separate sittings were devoted to them. Officials in every branch of the department were available and gave detailed answers to all the questions which the committee asked. The reports of those meetings are in printed form and are available to all hon. members as well as to any members of the public who are interested in securing them from the Queen's printer. The estimates of this department are never controversial, and we of the Liberal party see no need for a prolonged discussion of them at this time.
The minister has referred to the changes which have been brought about in the veterans charter and particularly to the amendments to the Pension Act and the War Veterans' Allowance Act which gave across the board 20 per cent increases to veterans. The hon. gentleman also mentioned the change in the regulations governing the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. We are grateful to the government for what it has done in this regard, and I am sure this has been much appreciated by veterans across Canada.
I am sure the minister will not mind my reminding him that there are still a few little jobs of tidying up which remain to be done. In particular, I have felt myself that the 365 day qualification with respect to service in the United Kingdom in connection with war veterans allowance by veterans of the first world war should be abolished. I think, also, that most veterans are agreed that something more should be done for the widows of veterans. In particular we feel that widows of Canadian citizens who served in the Imperial forces have a special case which merits consideration, and that it would be a good thing if the government could see its way clear to granting free medical treatment to pensioners and their families and to the widows of non-pensioners, too, and also to members of families of the war amputees. We would like to see the ceiling raised with respect to widows of non-pensioned veterans, and that under certain conditions they be

granted pensions as of right. I gather also that the people of Canada, and certainly most veterans organizations, would like to see a change brought about in the legislation so that damages which a widow might collect out of the accidental death of her husband would be treated as life assurance and other assets and not taken into account when the widow's rights to a pension are being considered.
I also think that changes should be made in the legislation whereby a veteran's pension would be made payable to his widow for a full year after his death, and an adequate allowance provided after that.
The committee received representations from many veterans organizations, including the Royal Canadian Legion, the national council of veterans associations of Canada, the war amps association, the Canadian non-pen-sioned widows association, and other veterans organizations. A study of the briefs submitted by those organizations indicated also unanimous agreement with these proposals. Practically every brief referred to each of these problems and recommended that something be done to correct them.
I must express my own disappointment that when the government was making amendments to the Canadian Pension Act and to the War Veterans' Allowance Act they did not embrace that opportunity to extend the benefits of the veterans charter to the merchant navy, to the rescue tug service, to the fire fighters and to the Newfoundland forestry units of world war II.
I know the minister will not expect me to sit down without reminding him again that the veterans of Newfoundland still are waiting for the necessary changes in legislation which will give them the status of those veterans who served in the Canadian forces, as was stipulated in the terms of union. As it is now the widows of Newfoundland veterans are in a different position from widows of other Canadian veterans. They have no rights. If they are granted pensions it is done as a favour and they forfeit their pensions if they leave the country. I ask the minister and the government to give urgent consideration to this measure and I express the hope that before too long the minister will find it possible to bring about further amendments to take care of those problems. This is all I need to say at this time. There are a few questions which I shall ask on the various items.

Supply-Veterans Affairs

I think my question could be put on item 456; it is related to items 456 and 457. Can the minister outline to the committee the policy of the department with respect to discovery of new treatments and of new drugs which might be available for the treatment of veterans in the hospitals operated under the Department of Veterans Affairs?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot give the hon. member specific instances but I have confidence that everything possible is being done with regard to changes, if necessary, in the treatment of veterans because they are so well served by a dedicated medical service across this country. The doctors who serve in our veterans' hospitals are men who are at the top of their profession. Many of them are also instructors or teachers in the medical schools of the universities. They comprise specialists in various aspects of medicine. They go beyond the call of duty in giving assistance to many of our veterans whether they are in hospital or not. Since they keep abreast of their profession, as I am sure they do, and I have met many of them, if any mode of new treatment becomes available it will be introduced. But I repeat what I said earlier; I have no specific instance to draw to the attention of the committee on this occasion.

Would it be apropos under this item to ask the minister just exactly what the department has in mind with respect to the operation of the veterans hospital which is now under construction as an annex to the General hospital in St. John's, Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The same purpose as was served elsewhere, namely to provide an increased number of beds for the treatment of people who require treatment; to improve the active bed situation and also to provide what is known as domiciliary care for people who qualify for that type of treatment in our veterans hospitals.
I do not think my question was understood. Does the department intend to operate the hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is attached to the St. John's General hospital as a pavilion and will be under the administration of that hospital.

In the past I have advocated an increase in the staff of pensions advocates, and particularly that full-time advocates be employed in Newfoundland. After looking over the situation over a number of years it has occurred to me that that might not be necessary; that we are now getting in this office in the various regions a personnel who are very experienced in handling veterans problems and in preparing their cases. I would ask the minister whether he would consider setting up a classification of personnel in which we might have assistant pensions advocates who might not have legal training but who, because of their experience in this work, might be able to do it just as capably and just as competently as members of the legal profession. This is just a suggestion that I would ask the minister to consider for the next year.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I will. As a matter of fact, I was talking about this subject with the deputy minister just yesterday. I had the opportunity of meeting the solicitors who are doing this work and who had assembled in Ottawa for a two-day conference. I had the opportunity of meeting them and talking to them, as did the parliamentary secretary, so that suggestion of the hon. member is under consideration at the present time.

461. War veterans allowance board-administration, $170,994.

There is just one point I should like to bring to the minister's attention with respect to recipients of war veterans allowance who are under the age of 60. In order for such a veteran to qualify he must somehow get a medical certificate to the effect that he is permanently unemployable. It seems to me that it is very difficult for a man to get such a certificate because in this day of rapid scientific advance, particularly in the medical field, it is most difficult to say that because a person has suffered from a disability for a number of years he will always suffer from it and that there is no chance of his ever improving to the point that he will be able to work. I suggest to the minister that if a person has been disabled for a number of years, say two or three, he should be considered as being sufficiently disabled to qualify for the war veterans allowance. His case could then be reviewed from year to year to see whether any improvement had taken place. I suggest that a person should not be barred until the age of 60 or until he can get somebody to certify that he is permanently disabled.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The problem is not new. It is an important one and has been given consideration in the past. The line is normally


drawn at age 60, of course, but there are quite a number of recipients under that age. As a matter of fact, over 4,000 are already on the roll who are under the age of 60. The war veterans allowance board has been very reasonable and lenient in considering these cases. I think it is important though to have this matter drawn to the attention of hon. members as the hon. member has done today. If instances occur where some member thinks that somebody requires attention and perhaps has not been getting it, I would ask the member to write me a letter about the matter and remind me of it again, if he does not get an immediate answer, and we will see that something is done.
