Having had the privilege of visiting the memorials at Vimy and Beau-mont-Hamel last July, I should like to take this opportunity to place on record my appreciation of the work that is being done by the department in caring for our memorials and graves of our war dead. I had the opportunity of seeing this at first hand and I was much impressed by what I saw. I am sure that parents, other relatives and friends who have loved ones resting over there will be very pleased to know that these graves are being cared for so well.
I should also like to take this opportunity to pay a special tribute to Mr. Allan Chambers, who also looked after the arrangements for the visit to the memorials, for the splendid work he is doing in this regard.

I have only one question which arises out of a case that came to my attention a short time ago. What is the policy with respect to a veteran who may have been deprived of benefits because of a wrong diagnosis on the part of the D.V.A. medical board that happened to examine the veteran? I have heard of a case where a wrong diagnosis was made on two occasions. On one occasion one diagnosis was made and 10 per cent disability was granted. On another occasion another diagnosis was made and 60 per cent disability was granted. On still another occasion the diagnosis was entirely different and 100 per cent disability was granted. Nothing in the veteran's condition had altered from the beginning to the end. The person was totally disabled right from the beginning and had to employ an attendant. It took several years before the

board actually made the correct diagnosis and awarded 100 per cent disability and an allowance for the attendant as well. Is it the policy of the department to reimburse veterans for losses they have incurred as a result of faulty diagnoses?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: In some instances the pension has been paid retroactively. The problem of diagnosis admittedly is difficult and I presume there are differences of opinion in that regard. However, the reexamination of anyone who is in doubt is always possible under the pension commission. The commission stands ready to assist in matters of this kind. If a veteran feels that on re-examination his case might be diagnosed somewhat differently, I presume it is perfectly all right for him to seek reexamination. In some instances but not in all the pension would be retroactive.

Before the vote carries I should like to mention something to the minister that came to my notice a few months ago. If a pensioner dies before the date in the month when the cheque has been received, the cheque for that month or part of the month that the pensioner was still alive cannot be cashed, naturally, but there is no payment made to the estate except on application and by grace. In the particular case to which I am referring this really did not matter at all, but it seems to me that there could be many cases where it would be really quite important that the pension should be paid. In my opinion it seems only reasonable and surely it was the intent of parliament that a pension that has been granted should be paid up to the date of the death of the person, even though it is only a fraction of a month. I do not know whether it is the law or whether it is merely a regulation but it does seem to me that this is something which might well be tidied up, not retroactively but for the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I was under the impression that was under control but we will look into the matter. My information is that the pension is payable up to the end of the month in which the person died. The head of the pension commission is here and is listening attentively. The matter will be looked into.
Item agreed to.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
This is the departmental administration item, and before it carries I should like to ask the minister if he would give a fuller explanation than he gave the Leader of the Opposition the other day as to why it is taking such a tremendously long time for the government to make up its mind what it is going to do about the Red river floodway in Manitoba?
Hon. W. G. Dinsdale (Minister of Northern
Affairs and National Resources): Mr. Chairman, I think the passage of time in respect of these matters is a matter of relativity. As a matter of fact the Winnipeg floodway project has been under discussion since about the year 1950 when the disaster flood occurred in the city of Winnipeg. As a Manitoban I was very much aware of the nature of the disaster that occurred even though my own city of Brandon was not affected directly by the flood. We did, at that time, feel the full impact of the refugee situation that was generated by the flood.
In the past decade there has been a continuing discussion as to how this recurring disaster to the city of Winnipeg might be dealt with, and it is only in recent years, since 1959 as a matter of fact, that a decision has been made to proceed with the Winnipeg floodway which was proposed by the factfinding committee set up at the time of the disaster. I believe considerable progress has been made on this matter. There is a joint committee of engineers representing the provincial government and our own federal government which has been working on the matter since last spring. They have made considerable progress in considering the engineering problems that arise in connection with a project as extensive as this one. Only in the past few days information has become available in this regard.
As to the matter of sharing the costs, we have had continuing discussions and negotiations on this important point. We have almost reached the point of agreement, but a special problem arose in this connection because, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate knows full well, this is an international river which rises south of the border. It cannot be regarded, therefore, as one which comes

Supply-Northern Affairs directly within the terms of the Canada Water Conservation Act which would be the act which would normally apply. This has meant that a special formula has to be worked out, and it is upon this problem we are working at the moment. As I indicated in reply to the Leader of the Opposition the other day, the discussions are proceeding very happily and we hope to make an announcement very shortly.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I read the Winnipeg newspapers and I suppose, like time, happiness is also a relative matter. I think perhaps the minister may be happier than the people with whom he is negotiating in Manitoba because the impression one gets from reading these newspapers is that the provincial government is anything but happy with the niggardly way they are being treated by the treasury, as compared with what they were led to expect before March 31, 1958. However, this is not the time to go into that subject.
In order to save time going into the matter on the next item, I should like to ask the minister on this item whether or not the department has in contemplation any special winter works program for national parks, such as it had last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman, we feel that there is a very strong necessity to continue our winter works program much along the same line as we have followed during recent years. This arises particularly from the tremendous upsurge in the numbers of people using the parks. We have preliminary statistics on tourism during the past summer which indicate that there is at least a 15 per cent increase across the board. Our parks have been packed to capacity. We have campsite extension programs under way in almost every one of the national parks and we hope to continue these works under the winter works program during the forthcoming winter.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to ask a question with regard to Rogers pass, having recently come over the route. I find that the federal government has practically completed their portion-that is the part in the national park -of the highway. But as you move eastward a very different story unfolds. You hit the province of British Columbia's part and at that stage it is not so good. I was wondering whether the minister could advise us if a date has been set for the opening of the highway. I should also like to ask what facilities will be available for the travelling public in the nature of camp sites and places to stop over night actually within the park limit.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member raised this point, Mr. Chairman. I have been quite concerned with the importance of the progress on the road through the Rogers pass, particularly in view of the fact that an important international fair gets under way in Seattle next year. This will be one of the main access routes to that fair. We think it will have a significant bearing on our tourist potential in that area.
As to the progress on the part of the highway through the national park, may I say this. We are giving special attention to this section. The hon. member will realize, of course, that this is the only section of the highway for which I have direct responsibility. However, we are hoping that it will be completed for use next summer, which would suggest that we could have an official opening ceremony some time in the early spring. We are fully aware of the situation. I am glad to have had this opportunity to bring the members of the committee up to date on the progress being made.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question while we are on this point. When I came down this fall I took the opportunity to drive through the park. The reason I am pressing this matter a little further, Mr. Chairman, in asking the minister if he knows the intention of the provincial government as to when they are going to open their portion is that work on the provincial portion of the road, to my own way of thinking, is so far behind that it will be practically impossible to open the road next year. I am wondering whether there is any correspondence on file in the minister's office from the provincial government in regard to their portion of the road.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This is the trans-Canada highway, of course; and, as such it comes under the responsibility of the Department of Public Works. I shall be happy to consult my colleague the Minister of Public Works and bring this query to his attention.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I have just one further question. Have we a budget for expenditures on campsites within the park limits for next year?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am sorry I neglected to answer that part of the hon. member's question. As he no doubt knows, the policy with regard to the construction of campsites and picnic sites along the trans-Canada highway is to have a picnic site every 50 miles and a campsite every one hundred miles. This policy will apply to the entire length of the trans-Canada highway.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
There is just one further matter. I hate to keep on pressing these things.

Having cleared up all the questions, may I say to the minister that I hope he will give heavy publicity to this Rogers pass route. It is a beautiful route through the Canadian rockies.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: There is just one question I should like to ask the minister. It comes under another vote in the supplementaries but I think I could ask it under vote 548. I raised it when the estimates of the Department of External Affairs were under consideration but I was not given a satisfactory answer. It has to do with the water levels at the port of Montreal, a matter which is a very serious one for that city. As the minister knows, there is a board of control. I think the chairman of that board of control is one of his officers. Can the minister tell me what is being done to provide the port of Montreal with a sufficient amount of water to take the kind of ships that it has been in the habit of taking? I refer to deep sea vessels. What provision is his department making to protect the down stream levels at Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This problem became a matter for consideration early in the year, as the hon. member will recall. At that time my department was consulted because of its responsibility in the field of water resources and one of our experts was assigned to the task of dealing with this difficulty. I must confess that I have not been in touch with the activities of this particular branch in the past week or so. If I can assist the hon. member I should be happy to send him a letter which provides up to date information as to where the matter stands.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I wonder whether I could just leave the matter this way so as not to delay the passage of the item. This is a matter of vital concern not only to the port of Montreal but to downstream interests. It is also a matter of vital concern to upstream interests. I am sure that the officers in question are doing their utmost, and that particularly the officer in the minister's department having to do with water resources is doing his utmost to put into effect a plan which will be satisfactory to all concerned. It so happens, however, that the plan is not satisfactory to all concerned and that it is causing grave prejudice to the rights to water resources first, for domestic and sanitary purposes and second, for navigation. These are the two branches as set out in the order of approval of the international joint commission. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and I ask him to see to it that there is put into effect a plan which will

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it has been the practice in the past-and I would not want to depart from it-to allow these estimates to go through without any discussion. It is certainly not my intention to hold them up, but perhaps the committee would allow me to just say a word in connection with the manner in which the Speaker has dealt with many of the representations which have been made to him from time to time by those of us who sit on this side of the chamber. I have reference now to not only the secretaries and the stenographers who look after our work, but to others as well.
I know it has not been possible for the Speaker to do everything he has wanted to do, but he has always been kind and considerate in his approach to the problems which we on this side of the chamber have brought to his attention. May I just add this, sir, and I will resume my seat.
As the Speaker knows, always during the period of recess some of the secretaries ana stenographers are without work. In this instance, it is not going to be too long until we meet again; it will only be a matter of two months because I understand there will be a new session of parliament in early December. It has been brought to my attention that because of the hardship that is being felt by some of these persons the Speaker might wish to give consideration to

allowing them to stay on for that short period of time. I wonder, Mr. Chairman, whether consideration could be given to that matter.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words, following the remarks of the hon. member who has just spoken, regarding the secretaries of the House of Commons. In so doing, I am sure hon. members will agree that they are all hard working and loyal, and that they deserve even greater recognition. It is therefore my intention to bring to the attention of the committee certain suggestions which I hope will not only improve their working conditions but will also help the members of parliament in the discharge of their responsibilities.
No doubt there will be some hon. members who will greet my suggestions with the reply that this is the way it has always been done. I do not have the advantage of knowing what conditions existed when we were in opposition, so I base my remarks purely on my own experience since I was elected in 1957.
When I first came to Ottawa, Mr. Chairman, I was under the impression that parliament at the most sat for six or seven months out of each year. Those who were employed as secretaries to the members of parliament understood, therefore, that there would be a period of five or six months when they would not be employed by parliament and that it would be their own responsibility to find other employment or just take a holiday. For a long time we had a considerable number of married women on the staff who found this arrangement quite satisfactory because it enabled them to supplement the family income and during the adjournment they were able to spend a few months at home.
I believe the situation has now changed and that a very large number of single girls are now employed who, as the hon. member for Laurier said, because of the irregular pattern of the sessions of parliament find it extremely difficult to make plans for other employment. Under the best of circumstances, when our secretaries go to the civil service to look for other employment during the recess or adjournment they take a considerable cut in pay, even though because of the experience they have received in the House of Commons they are given greater responsibility than other girls in the civil service with whom they work.
I can understand the reluctance of the civil service to employ secretaries from parliament hill because they can in no way be considered permanent employees. But even so, the girls who need work do not object too strenuously to this arrangement because there is at least other employment.

However, in these last two sessions of parliament more secretaries have experienced difficulty in finding work with the civil service because the recess and the adjournment have been so short that the civil service did not even want to hire them. It may be answered, Mr. Chairman, that these girls can draw unemployment insurance, but I have received a number of complaints from secretaries who filed their claim on the day parliament went into recess last July but who had to wait almost a month before they received their first unemployment insurance cheque. I wrote to the Minister of Labour about this, and after he looked into the situation, he confirmed that some benefit payments had been delayed because the records of contribution had not been forwarded to the local unemployment insurance commission office. Surely, we have had enough experience with recesses and adjournments that a secretary need not suffer any embarrassment caused by waiting for her unemployment insurance. In this connection I have been assured by the Minister of Labour that a close watch will be kept on the situation so that it will not happen again.
The argument has been put forward that the rates of pay for the secretaries of the House of Commons are deliberately fixed higher than those received by other secretaries working for private firms so that they are compensated somewhat for periods of unemployment. I suggest that this is unfair, because no matter what salary you give to our secretaries they only receive that rate for the number of months during which they are employed, and the extra salary they receive in no way compensates for the months during which they are unemployed; neither does it help to make up the salary which they receive during the adjournment from the civil service to the level of the remuneration which they receive when working in the House of Commons. At the same time, there might be some secretaries who are not as highly qualified as we would like them to be, or according to civil service standards, but that is the fault of the member of parliament for hiring her and not the fault of the girl.
It has also been said that these secretaries do not have to work in the House of Commons if they are dissatisfied with the conditions. I feel that this statement is not quite fair, because these girls would be the first to admit that they enjoy their work here, and surely we should not take advantage of their desire to work for us. None of us has to be here, but we are here because we want to be here. If we find a girl who is a topnotch secretary we want to keep her, but unless we can offer her better working conditions I am very much afraid that they will be forced

through economic reasons to look for employment elsewhere. We all realize that it takes a long time to train a secretary so that she becomes familiar with your own work, and that is another reason why we should make it attractive for her to stay on at the House of Commons.
I repeat that under ordinary circumstances and with shorter sessions, the problem of secretaries would not be as great. However, with longer sessions the problem is very urgent. Lest it be thought that 1 am thinking only of the welfare of the secretaries, let me emphasize that I am also concerned with the efficiency of the members of parliament in the discharge of their duties, and our efficiency is lessened by not having our secretaries available for work during our evening sessions; by not having secretaries during the recess and adjournment, and by not having dictating machines so that we can put work on tape for our secretaries. I am sure that all of us recall the earlier part of this session when many were attending committee meetings which started at 9 or 9.30 a.m., and then going to the House of Commons at 11 a.m. If we spent all our time sitting in the house, which did not rise until 10.30 p.m., there was no time left to look after our correspondence. If we had dictating machines, many of us could do a lot of work in the evenings, particularly when we sit from 7.30 p.m. to 10.30 p.m., when the secretaries have gone home.
We have now reached a stage where the government has recognized that it is in the interest of greater efficiency that each member of parliament should have his own secretary. This is a very recent move but I think that it recognizes that improvements were overdue. I suggest we should now carry these changes one step further by granting to each member of parliament an allowance for a secretary who would be on a full time basis, which allowance would also be sufficient to cover her travel expenses to and from the House of Commons from her home. It would then be up to the member to decide if he wants to employ her only when the house is in session or if he also wants her to work in his own constituency. There might be a danger of different salaries being offered by individual members of parliament but I think a standard contract could be worked out. I also think the member of parliament should still have the privilege of recommending a girl for employment as his secretary, although the House of Commons would do the actual hiring.
I think that by having a secretary on a full time basis, we would have greater efficiency and continuity. I am sure hon. mem-

bers will appreciate how difficult it is to get any work done while the house is in recess or while it is adjourned, and if you do not have a secretary in your own office, it is very difficult, if not impossible, to make any replies or do any work satisfactorily.
I think we should also bring the salary range into line with those received by secretaries assigned to the other place. For example, a secretary to a member of parliament must wait five full sessions before she reaches the maximum rate of pay. Secretaries in the other place, however, reach their full maximum after only three sessions. In my opinion, secretaries in the House of Commons work a great deal harder and are under much greater pressure, and I see no reason why there should be this disparity.
The government of Canada is the biggest business in the country. Surely we can apply good business methods of administration to running this colossal undertaking. In my discussions back home I have pointed out some of the problems facing members of parliament, and I always received the classic answer "You are in power now, why don't you do something about it?" I believe that by assigning a secretary to each member of parliament the government recognizes the need of some improvement. I think the suggestions I have made are consistent steps, and if sessions keep up the way they do then I suggest it is time we consider parliament being placed on a full year basis at it is in England.
Certainly, I personally find that because of the nature of the present sessions, my law practice in Vancouver is completely lost and so I might as well devote my time to politics. And if I am to devote my full time to politics, I may as well become a professional in this field, because government is now so complex that it is no place for amateurs. We no longer dabble in politics as if it were a hobby. We work very hard at it.
I think that if the government were to implement my suggestions, the over-all cost of administration would not be great. The secretaries would be much happier; their morale would increase considerably and, equally important, I think the work output for each member of parliament would reflect this increased efficiency.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
So that I shall not lose en-tierly this single opportunity of the year to speak from the floor of the house, I want to thank the hon. member for Laurier for his very generous reference to my administration of the staff of the House of Commons. I also

wish to thank the other members who have spoken for their very constructive suggestions which it will be of great pleasure to take into account and bring before the commissioners of internal economy, particularly at this time when consideration is being given to new estimates and an opportunity is available to make good some of the deficiencies.
The administrative responsibilities are substantial, but I have enjoyed the assistance of a very competent staff. I should like to thank them and to pay my tribute to the Clerk of the house and to his assistants, to the Sergeant-at-Arms, to the legislative council and to all the chiefs of the various branches of the house and their respective staffs.
The continuous staff are, I think, particularly badly off because in this unusual session perhaps they have not received the compensation which would make good to them the extra time they put in when the house sits for long hours over many months, inasmuch as such compensation is not adequate for the pattern which this particular session has taken. A good deal of thought has been given and is being given to what alternatives are possible not only for the continuous staff but for the sessional staff to which the hon. member for Laurier and, as well, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre made reference. It is true that many of those who work here sessionally do it by preference because they like part-time work; but there are many others who are working sessionally who are dependent upon their earnings for their livelihood. How to meet that difficulty is a problem. If sessions are to be as long as this one, we suggest that perhaps when we are sitting most of the year consideration might be given to an annual rate. It is true that the sessional rate has been rather better than the normal rate because of the disadvantage of a period of recess.
Various alternatives are being presented. One alternative proposed is for parliament to adopt the procedure of sitting at regular times so that those who work in parliament will know when they will be employed and when they will not. Another alternative suggested for consideration is that of an annual rate. With respect to stenographers, another suggestion is that an allowance might be made to members which will enable them to supply themselves with stenographic service the year round.
In any event, I think hon. members will agree that during the latter part of this session we have improved the service to the extent that every member who required stenographic service has been able to receive it.
I do not want to break the rules myself.
